High-low rigs with small hooks and clam pieces are producing steady action in 25 to 35 feet. The fish are running large — plenty of 12-inchers mixed with the usual 8 to 10-inch fish.

What's interesting is how the spring tides are affecting the bite timing. Normally I'd expect the best action around slack water, but these big currents are keeping the bait moving and the fish active throughout the tide cycle. The bass especially seem to be feeding aggressively when the current is at its strongest, using the flow to their advantage.

Water clarity has been excellent despite all the current movement. The lack of significant rainfall this month means no muddy runoff, and the strong tides are actually cleaning up any debris that might have settled during the neap tide period two weeks ago.

Looking ahead, we're moving into the waning moon phase, which should moderate these extreme tides somewhat. But the water temperature is in that perfect 65 to 70-degree range where everything feeds aggressively. The real wildcard will be whether this weather pattern holds — these light southwest winds have been perfect for fishing the shoals and deeper structure.

I'm particularly watching for the first push of bonito, which typically show up in the deeper water off Stratford Shoal around the third week of June. The bait concentration we're seeing now, combined with the temperature structure, could set up an early run if conditions stay stable. The key will be watching for diving birds and surface activity in the 50 to 80-foot zone east of the shoal.

For the weekend, focus on the structure during the stronger tide phases. The spring tide influence will carry through Sunday, so plan your trips around the current rather than fighting it. Early morning and late afternoon continue to be prime time, especially when the tide change coincides with low light conditions.

reports.headline: Bass blitz fires the western Sound as bunker schools stack thick off Matinecock
reports.subhead: Slot fish crushing live peanuts on the flood tide while fluke fishing stays tough in the shallows.
reports.body_markdown:
The western Sound finally woke up this week, and when it did, it came alive with a vengeance. After weeks of scratching for fish, the bunker schools that should have been here in May finally showed up off Matinecock Point, and the bass followed like they were reading from the same playbook I've been watching for three decades.

The action kicked off Tuesday morning when the first real schools of peanut bunker pushed into the bay on the flood tide. By Wednesday, you couldn't miss them — thick clouds of bait stacked up from the Matinecock flats all the way to the Stepping Stones. The bass moved in right behind them, and suddenly every boat from here to City Island was marking fish.

I've been working the 25 to 35-foot zone off Matinecock on the incoming water, and it's been lights out for slot fish. These aren't the schoolies we've been picking at all spring — we're talking solid 28 to 32-inch bass that are feeding hard on those peanuts. Live-lining the bunker on a simple fishfinder rig with a 6/0 circle hook has been the ticket. Keep your sinker light — just enough to get down in the current — and let that bait swim naturally in the tide.

The key has been timing the flood tide right. Start fishing about an hour before the turn and work through the first three hours of incoming water. The bass are staging on the channel edges where the deep water meets the flats, ambushing bait as it gets pushed up by the current. I've been finding the best action in 28 to 32 feet, right where the bottom starts to slope up toward the shallows.

Execution Rocks has been producing too, especially on the back side where the current breaks around the structure. The outgoing tide there has been money — bass are sitting in the eddy waiting for bait to get swept past. Same rig setup, but you need a bit more weight to hold bottom in that current. Three-ounce bank sinkers have been perfect.

The Throgs Neck Bridge pilings are holding fish on both tides, but you've got to be precise with your positioning. Work the up-current side of the pilings on the flood, the down-current side on the ebb. The bass are using that structure to break the current and conserve energy while they feed. Bucktails tipped with pork rind have been deadly when the live bait bite slows down — 1-ounce white bucktails bounced along the bottom.

Fluke fishing, on the other hand, has been a grind. The water's warming up nicely — hitting 68 degrees in the back bays — but the flatfish just aren't cooperating yet. I'm marking plenty of shorts in the usual spots off Lloyd Neck and the Huntington flats, but keepers are few and far between. The few decent fish I've seen came on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted slow in 20 to 25 feet of water.

The problem with the fluke bite seems to be bait-related. There's plenty of spearing and small snappers around, but not the sand eels and larger baits that really get the big fluke excited. Until we see more substantial forage move in, it's going to stay a pick-and-choose game with the summer flounder.

Porgies have been a bright spot for family fishing. The reefs around Hart Island and the structure off Sands Point have been loaded with scup in the 10 to 14-inch range. High-low rigs baited with clam or squid strips work best. Fish the bottom on the slack tides when the current isn't ripping too hard.

Looking ahead, this new moon cycle should keep the bass bite hot. The spring tides are going to push more bait around, and with water temperatures climbing into the low 70s, we should see even more activity. I'm watching for the bunker schools to spread east toward Huntington and west toward the Bronx — when that happens, this whole western Sound is going to explode.

The weekend looks promising with light winds and calm seas. Get out there early, find the bait, and you'll find the fish. After a slow start to the season, the western Sound is finally fishing like June should feel.

reports.headline: Yellowfin blitz fires Veatch Canyon as warm water pushes north
reports.subhead: Chunking at dawn produces 60-pound class fish while trollers find wahoo in the blue water.
reports.body_markdown:
The eastern canyons came alive this week as a push of 72-degree water moved up from the south, stacking bait and firing the yellowfin bite at Veatch Canyon. I've been running out of Montauk and Block Island, and the fishing has been as good as I've seen it in early June.

Veatch has been the star performer. The 30-fathom line is holding consistent 71-degree water, a solid 6-degree break from the inshore stuff. That thermal edge is concentrating skipjack and small bluefin, which in turn has the yellowfin feeding aggressively at first light. We're finding fish from 40 to 80 pounds on the chunk, working fresh butterfish and squid on circle hooks. The key is getting there before sunrise — by 7 AM the bite shuts down as the fleet arrives and the fish sound.

Trolling the canyon edges has been producing wahoo in that same warm water. High-speed spreads with blue-and-white Ilanders and ballyhoo combinations are getting hit hard, especially along the 100-fathom contour where the current creates upwelling. The wahoo are running 25 to 40 pounds, typical for this time of year, but they're aggressive and numerous.

Hydrographer Canyon is fishing well for smaller yellowfin and some nice mahi. The weed lines have been sparse, but where you find them, they're holding dolphin to 15 pounds. Live bait has been king here — we're catching our own tinker mackerel on the ride out and fishing them on light tackle. The mahi are spooky in the clear water, so long leaders and careful boat positioning matter.

Atlantis Canyon has been tougher, but the few boats making the run are finding bigeye tuna in the deep water. Night fishing with squid on the bottom has produced fish to 150 pounds, though it's a grind. The current has been ripping through there, making it tough to hold bottom, but when you can get your baits down, the fish are there.

The water clarity has been exceptional — that gin-clear blue that makes you want to dive in. Visibility is pushing 100 feet in the canyons, which means the fish can see everything. We've had to go to longer leaders and smaller hooks to get bites. Fluorocarbon has been essential, especially for the wahoo that seem to inspect everything twice.

Bait has been the story this week. The skipjack schools are thick from the 20-fathom line out to the canyon walls. We're seeing massive marks on the sounder, and the yellowfin are feeding on them hard. Fresh butterfish from the Fulton Fish Market has been outproducing everything else for chunking, though good squid runs a close second.

The moon phase is working in our favor — we're three days past new, so the tides are building toward springs. That increased current flow is pushing nutrients up the canyon walls and concentrating bait. The best fishing has been on the incoming tide, especially that first hour after slack water when the current starts to build.

Weather has been cooperative with light southwest winds and 2-foot seas. The ride out to Veatch is 35 miles from Montauk, manageable in most boats, though I'd recommend 28 feet or bigger for comfort. From Block Island, it's a shorter run to the northern canyons, and several boats are making day trips successfully.

Looking ahead, the extended forecast shows this weather pattern holding through the weekend. The warm water should stay put, and with the moon building toward full, I expect the bite to intensify. The spring tides will flush more bait out of the inshore waters, and that usually means better canyon fishing. I'm planning to hit Veatch again at first light Friday, then work south to Hydrographer if the yellowfin bite slows. The key is staying mobile and following the temperature breaks — that's where the fish will be.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Yellowfin explosion at Spencer as warm water pushes north from the Gulf Stream
reports.subhead: Norfolk and Lindenkohl firing on live bunker as 72-degree water holds bait tight to the ledges.
reports.body_markdown:
The southern canyons are absolutely on fire right now, and it's all about that warm water push we've been waiting for. Spencer Canyon has been the star of the show this week, with yellowfin tuna in the 40 to 80-pound class crushing everything from cedar plugs to live bunker. The key has been working the 100-fathom line where that beautiful 72-degree water is sitting — a solid 6 degrees warmer than what we were seeing just two weeks ago.

I've been running out of Ocean City at first light, hitting Spencer's northeast wall where the current breaks and creates that perfect feeding zone. The yellowfin are stacked between 80 and 120 feet of water, and they're not picky. Chunking with fresh bunker has been deadly — cut the bunker into 4-inch pieces, hook them through the back on a 7/0 circle hook with a 3-foot fluorocarbon leader, and let them drift back in the slick. The key is keeping that chum line going steady. These fish are aggressive right now, but they want to see that constant stream of bait.

Trolling has been equally productive, especially early morning and late afternoon. I've been pulling a spread of cedar plugs and ballyhoo — the Yo-Zuri Bonita in blue and silver has been absolutely crushing them. Run them at 7 to 8 knots, and don't be afraid to work the edges where the clean blue water meets that slightly greener inshore stuff. That's where the bait gets concentrated, and that's where the yellowfin are feeding.

Norfolk Canyon has been the sleeper hit this week. The 30 to 50-pound yellowfin are thick on the southern edge, and I'm seeing some nice wahoo mixed in — fish in the 25 to 40-pound range that are absolutely smoking high-speed trollers. If you're targeting wahoo specifically, get your speed up to 12 knots and pull wire line with Ilander-ballyhoo combos. The purple and black Ilanders have been money, especially the 9-inch size.

Lindenkohl has been producing steady action on both yellowfin and some surprising bluefin. The bluefin are smaller — 20 to 40-pound fish — but they're hungry and willing to eat. I've been finding them on the northwest corner where the canyon wall drops from 60 to 200 fathoms. Live bunker on a fishfinder rig has been the ticket, but you need to get them down to where the fish are holding. Use a 2-ounce egg sinker and let that bait swim naturally in the current.

The mahi bite has been inconsistent but worth targeting when you find them. I've been seeing scattered schools of 5 to 15-pound fish around floating debris and weed lines, particularly between Spencer and Norfolk. Small ballyhoo on light tackle has been fun, but the real trick is finding the floating structure. Look for anything — logs, pallets, even thick weed lines — and work them thoroughly.

Poor Man's Canyon has been the toughest of the four this week, but it's still producing fish. The yellowfin here seem to be deeper and more scattered, requiring more patience and precise boat positioning. I've had my best luck on the eastern edge where the canyon starts to shallow up, working depths between 100 and 150 fathoms.

The water temperature has been the real story this week. That Gulf Stream push has brought consistent 72-degree water right up to the canyon edges, and it's holding there. This is exactly what we need to see for sustained action through the summer. The bait is thick — I'm marking huge schools of bunker, herring, and squid on the fishfinder, and that's what's keeping these pelagics around.

Looking ahead, this weekend's new moon should create some serious tidal movement, which typically fires up the bite even more. I'm expecting the yellowfin action to continue strong, and I wouldn't be surprised to see some white marlin start showing up as we get deeper into June. The water temperature trend looks stable, so plan on this pattern holding for at least another week.

reports.headline: Washington Canyon fires early as warm eddies stack yellowfin on the northwest wall
reports.subhead: 68-degree water and scattered bunker pods trigger first real tuna bite of the season.
reports.body_markdown:
The Washington came alive this week like I haven't seen in early June for three seasons. Water temps spiked to 68 degrees along the northwest wall where that persistent eddy has been spinning, a solid 6 degrees warmer than the surrounding blue water. That temperature break is pure gold this time of year — it's concentrating bait and firing up the first real yellowfin bite of 2026.

I've been watching this setup develop for ten days now. The Gulf Stream pushed a warm core ring north, and when it collided with the canyon's northwest shoulder, it created this beautiful thermal pocket that's been holding steady all week. The yellowfin moved in Tuesday, and by Thursday we had boats working steady action from the 100-fathom curve all the way up to the 60-line.

The fish are running 30 to 60 pounds — classic early-season Washington yellowfin. They're not the monsters we'll see in August, but they're fat, aggressive, and absolutely hammering anything that looks like a bunker. Spreader bars with cedar plugs are producing the most consistent action, especially the natural wood finish with silver mylar. I'm running them 150 feet back on the long riggers, and when you see that rod tip bounce twice and then load up hard, you know you've got a yellowfin coming to the boat.

Live bunker is absolutely deadly when you can find them. The key is getting them down to the 40-foot mark where the fish are feeding. I'm using a 6/0 circle hook through the nose, 80-pound fluorocarbon leader, and just enough weight to get the bait down without killing it. The yellowfin are coming up from 80 feet to hit these baits, and the strikes are violent — no mistaking a tuna bite for anything else.

Chunking has been productive too, especially on the evening bite. Fresh bunker chunks on 8/0 circles, fished on the drift along the temperature break. The trick is reading the current — when that eddy is spinning clockwise, you want to position yourself on the upstream side and let your chunks sweep into the warmer water. I've seen boats limit out in two hours working this pattern.

The bluefin are mixed in, mostly smaller fish in the 40 to 80-pound range. They're hitting the same baits as the yellowfin, but they're more finicky about presentation. Slow down your trolling speed to 6 knots, and make sure your spread looks natural. These early-season bluefin have seen a lot of boats, and they'll turn away from anything that doesn't look right.

Mahi showed up Wednesday in decent numbers, mostly along the eastern edge where the water drops from blue to deep blue. They're schoolie fish, 5 to 15 pounds, but they're aggressive and fun on light tackle. Small cedar plugs and ballyhoo combinations are working best. Once you hook the first one, keep the boat in gear and work the school — these fish are traveling in tight groups.

Bait situation is interesting this week. The bunker pods are scattered but consistent, mostly along the 30 to 50-fathom line. They're not the massive schools we'll see later in the season, but there's enough bait to keep the tuna interested. I'm also seeing good numbers of flying fish, which explains why the mahi are so active.

Looking ahead, this weekend's new moon should really fire things up. Spring tides always seem to concentrate bait along the canyon walls, and with water temperatures holding steady in the high 60s, I expect the yellowfin bite to get even better. The weather looks cooperative through Sunday, with light southwest winds and 2-foot seas.

My advice for anyone heading out: focus on that northwest wall between the 60 and 100-fathom lines. Watch your fish finder for the temperature break — when you see that 4 to 6-degree jump, that's where you want to fish. And bring plenty of ice — when the Washington fires this early in the season, it usually fires hard.

reports.headline: Yellowfin blitz fires at the Wilmington as Gulf Stream eddy locks in
reports.subhead: 68-degree water spinning off the main current has tuna stacked thick from the 30 line to the wall.
reports.body_markdown:
The Wilmington Canyon is absolutely on fire right now, and it's all about that warm-core eddy that spun off the Gulf Stream and parked itself right where we want it. Water temps jumped from 62 to 68 degrees in three days, and the yellowfin responded like someone rang the dinner bell.

I've been running this canyon for fifteen years, and when you see that temperature gradient lock up like this — cold 62-degree water on the inshore side, 68-degree Gulf Stream water spinning in a tight eddy from the 100 fathom curve out to the wall — you know it's game time. The bait got compressed against that thermal barrier, and the yellowfin moved in to feed.

Tuesday's trip told the whole story. We started chunking at first light on the 30 line where the temperature break was sharpest, using fresh butterfish and squid on 6/0 circles with 60-pound fluorocarbon leaders. Within an hour we had our first yellowfin in the boat — a solid 45-pounder that took a butterfish chunk 40 feet down on the drift. By noon we'd boated six more, all between 35 and 55 pounds, with two fish pushing the 60-pound mark.

The key right now is reading that eddy structure. It's not a perfect circle — it's more like a kidney shape running northeast to southwest, with the warmest water concentrated along the eastern edge where it's spinning fastest. That's where the bait gets trapped, and that's where you want to set up your drift. I'm seeing the best action from 0600 to 1000, then again from 1500 to sunset when the current shifts and repositions the bait.

Trolling has been equally productive for crews who want to cover water. The yellowfin are scattered throughout the eddy, not just stacked on the edges, so you can run spreads and pick them up consistently. Cedar plugs and small feathers in the 6 to 8-inch range are getting crushed, especially anything with blue and white or green and yellow. I'm pulling them at 6.5 to 7 knots, which seems to be the sweet spot for these fish.

The mahi bite has been a nice bonus. They're riding the weed lines that form along the current breaks, particularly where the eddy water meets the cooler inshore flow. Nothing huge — most fish running 10 to 20 pounds — but they're aggressive and willing to eat both trolled baits and chunks. A few boats reported white marlin mixed in with the mahi schools, though I haven't seen them personally.

What's really encouraging is the bait situation. There's a solid population of flying fish, squid, and small tunas throughout the eddy, which means this isn't just a quick hit-and-run scenario. When you see that kind of forage base established in warm water, the predators tend to stick around and feed heavily.

The weather window looks good through the weekend, with light southwest winds and seas under three feet. That eddy should hold its position for at least another week — these warm-core features don't just disappear overnight, especially when they're as well-defined as this one. The real question is whether it stays stationary or starts drifting northeast toward the Hudson Canyon.

My read on the water tells me we're in the sweet spot of a classic June yellowfin bite. The Gulf Stream is running strong and close, the water temperature differential is creating perfect feeding conditions, and the fish are here in numbers. If you've been thinking about making the run to the Wilmington, this is your week.

Looking ahead, I'm watching the moon phase — we're approaching new moon on the 18th, which typically means stronger tidal flows and more active feeding. Combined with this eddy structure, I expect the bite to stay strong through next weekend. The only variable is weather — there's a front tracking toward us early next week that could stir things up, but for now, it's as good as it gets out here.

reports.headline: Yellowfin blitz fires the canyon wall as 72-degree water holds bait tight
reports.subhead: Big eyes pushing up from the deep as thermal breaks stack everything on the 100-fathom line.
reports.body_markdown:
The canyon is absolutely on fire right now, and it's all about that 72-degree water sitting tight against the wall. I've been running out here for twenty-three years, and when you see that kind of thermal gradient — 68 degrees on the shelf dropping to 72 at the break — you know the yellowfin are going to stack up like cordwood.

We've been finding them consistently between the 100-fathom line and the Claw, mostly in that 180 to 220-foot zone where the warm water meets the upwelling. The fish are running 40 to 80 pounds, with a few pushing the century mark. Cedar plugs and spreader bars are getting crushed on the troll, but the real action is happening when you stop the boat and chunk.

Here's the deal: these fish are feeding on squid that are getting pushed up by the thermal break. I'm running a simple fishfinder rig with a 6/0 circle hook, 4 feet of 80-pound fluorocarbon, and chunks of fresh squid about the size of your thumb. Drop it back 150 feet behind the boat and let it flutter down through the water column. The takes are violent — these yellowfin are absolutely crushing the baits.

The bigeye situation is even more interesting. They're coming up from the deep water at first light and again right at sunset, probably following that same squid migration. I'm seeing them in 300 to 400 feet of water, just off the main canyon wall. These fish are bigger — 80 to 120 pounds — and they want the bait presented differently. I'm using a sliding sinker rig with just enough weight to get down, maybe 8 ounces, and letting the squid chunk drift naturally in the current.

The mahi bite has been solid too, especially around any floating debris you can find. We picked up a dozen fish between 10 and 25 pounds yesterday, all on ballyhoo rigged behind small feathers. The key is working the edges of the weed lines where they intersect with the temperature breaks. These fish are aggressive right now — they'll hit just about anything that moves.

What's really driving this bite is the way the Gulf Stream is interacting with the shelf water. That 72-degree tongue is pushing right up against the canyon wall, creating a perfect feeding zone. The bait — mostly squid, some small tunas, and scattered flying fish — is getting concentrated right where we want to fish. It's textbook canyon fishing when everything lines up like this.

The white marlin have been showing up sporadically, mostly on the troll. I'm running a spread of ballyhoo behind sea witches, working the 150 to 200-foot zone where the color change is most pronounced. These fish are finicky — you need to keep the baits moving and stay alert for that telltale bill slashing behind the spread.

Timing is critical out here right now. The best bite has been happening in that first hour after sunrise and again in the last two hours before dark. The fish seem to shut down during the heat of the day, probably because the bait drops deeper when the sun gets high. I'm adjusting my fishing times accordingly — early launch, long run, fish hard during the prime windows.

The current has been running pretty steady at about 1.5 knots to the northeast, which is perfect for drifting and chunking. Any faster and it becomes hard to keep your baits in the zone; any slower and the fish seem less aggressive. This current speed lets you cover water while keeping your presentation natural.

Looking ahead, I'm watching the weather pattern closely. We've got a front moving through this weekend that should stir things up and potentially push some fresh bait into the canyon. The new moon is coming up next week, which typically means stronger currents and more active feeding. If this thermal structure holds together through the weekend, we could be looking at some of the best canyon fishing of the early season.

The key right now is being flexible with your approach and paying attention to what the fish are telling you. Some days they want the baits trolled fast, other days they want them chunked slow. But with water this good and bait this concentrated, the canyon is fishing as well as I've seen it in years.

reports.headline: Raritan Bay stripers crash bunker schools as June water hits prime temps
reports.subhead: Big bass feeding heavy on peanut bunker from Sandy Hook to Manasquan as bait migration peaks.
reports.body_markdown:
The Raritan Bay is absolutely loaded right now, and I mean stacked with stripers from 28 to 40 inches that are feeding like they haven't eaten in weeks. Water temps hit that magic 68-degree mark this week, and the bunker schools are so thick you can smell them from the dock at Keyport.

I've been working the back bay from the Amboy channel markers to the Outerbridge, and it's been lights-out fishing on the moving water. These fish are crushing peanut bunker on fishfinder rigs — 3/0 circle hooks on 30-pound leader, just enough weight to get down in the 15 to 20 feet of water where the bait is stacked. The key is fishing the edges of the bunker schools, not right in the middle where the fish are spooked.

The bite has been best on the last two hours of the incoming and first hour of the ebb. That's when the current pushes the bait against the channel edges and the bass set up to ambush. I'm seeing guys limit out on keeper bass using live peanuts, but the chunk bait bite has been just as good. Fresh bunker chunks on a 6/0 circle hook, fished on a three-way rig with a 2-ounce sinker, is putting fish in the boat from dawn to about 10 AM.

What's really got me fired up is the size of these fish. We're not talking schoolies here — these are legitimate keeper bass with plenty of 32 to 36-inch fish mixed in. The biomass that moved into the bay this week is incredible, and it's all following the bunker migration that's been building since late May.

Down at Manasquan Inlet, the jetty bite has been solid for guys working the rocks on the outgoing tide. White bucktails with pork rind trailers in the 1 to 2-ounce range are getting hit hard in the 8 to 12 feet of water along the north jetty. The trick is keeping your jig moving — these fish want action, not a dead stick presentation.

The fluke bite has been decent but not spectacular. Shark River has been producing short fish on Gulp Swimming Mullets in white and chartreuse, but the keeper ratio is maybe one in ten. The better fluke action is outside in 25 to 30 feet, but you're competing with the sea bass that are absolutely crushing everything that hits bottom.

Speaking of sea bass, if you've got a New Jersey license, get out there now. The 10-fish limit runs through June 19, and these fish are stacked on every piece of structure from the Shrewsbury Rocks to the Axel Carlson Reef. Drop a clam or piece of squid on a high-low rig and you'll be bent over in seconds. I'm seeing guys boat 50 fish in a morning and keep their 10 best.

The weakfish bite has been spotty but promising. A few fish in the 16 to 20-inch range have been taken on small bucktails with Gulp baits in the back bays, especially around the Navesink River mouth on the evening tides. These fish are finicky — you need light tackle and a subtle presentation.

Looking at the moon phase, we're building toward a new moon on June 18, which means the spring tides are going to really move water through these inlets. That's when I expect the weakfish bite to really turn on, and the striper action should stay hot as long as the bunker schools hold in the bay.

The water clarity has been excellent — that gin-clear water that lets you see bottom in 15 feet. Combined with the perfect temperature gradient between the bay and ocean, we've got textbook conditions for a sustained bite.

Next week, I'm watching for the bunker to start moving south toward Barnegat Bay. When that happens, the Manasquan and Shark River inlets are going to be absolutely insane on the outgoing tides. Get your live bait game dialed in and be ready to run and gun with the schools.

reports.headline: Bay fluke fire as water hits 68 — bucktails and Gulp dominating the drift
reports.subhead: Marine Parkway Bridge producing keeper doormat action on the outgoing tide.
reports.body_markdown:
The bay finally woke up this week, and it's been worth the wait. Water temps climbed to 68 degrees in the back channels — a solid jump from last week's 64 — and that thermal shift has the fluke stacked up like cordwood on the deeper edges.

I've been working the Marine Parkway Bridge area hard, and the fish are responding. Best action comes on the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current sweeps bait off the flats and concentrates it in the channel. I'm talking keeper fluke to 6 pounds, with plenty of 18-to-20-inch fish mixed in. The sweet spot is that 25-to-30-foot drop right where the bridge shadow ends — the fish are sitting on that edge waiting for the tide to deliver dinner.

Rig-wise, it's been all about the bucktail-and-teaser combo. Three-quarter-ounce white bucktails tipped with 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets in pearl, with a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp grub on a teaser hook 18 inches up the line. Drag it slow on the drift — let the current do the work. The fish want that bait moving just fast enough to flutter, not racing across the bottom like you're trying to catch a cab.

The Cross Bay Bridge has been producing too, especially on the incoming when bait gets pushed up against the pilings. I've been anchoring uptide and casting bucktails into the current seams. Same rig, but bump up to a full ounce to hold bottom in the stronger flow. Had a beautiful 4-pounder there Tuesday morning that absolutely crushed a white Gulp on the drop.

Weakfish are making their presence known too — not the numbers we used to see, but quality fish in the 16-to-20-inch range. They're hitting the same bucktail rigs, but they want it worked a little more aggressively. Lift and drop, lift and drop, keeping contact with bottom but giving that jig some action. Found them staging in the deeper holes behind Canarsie Pier, where the cooler bay water meets the warmer backwater.

Bait situation is solid. Plenty of spearing and juvenile bunker in the shallows, which explains why the bass are starting to show. I've seen some nice 24-to-28-inch stripers mixed in with the fluke, especially around the bridge pilings on the flood tide. They're not in full feeding mode yet, but they're there. Give it another week of warm weather and we should see some real action.

Porgies are thick as thieves on any structure — bridge pilings, old dock remains, even the deeper shell beds. High-low rigs with small hooks and clam or sandworm pieces. Nothing fancy, just good eating fish to fill the cooler while you wait for fluke bites.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon this weekend, which means spring tides and stronger current flow. That should really fire up the bite, especially if this warm weather holds. I'm watching for that first real push of bunker into the bay — when that happens, the bass fishing is going to explode. The signs are all there: bait moving, water warming, and fish positioning on the structure. It's shaping up to be a hell of a summer on Jamaica Bay.

reports.headline: Jones Inlet fluke bite heats up as bay water climbs past 65 degrees
reports.subhead: Doormat season kicks into gear with keepers coming from the Meadowbrook drift and inlet mouth.
reports.body_markdown:
The fluke fishing around Jones Inlet finally turned the corner this week, and it's about damn time. Bay water hit 66 degrees Tuesday — a solid jump from the 62 we've been stuck on for weeks — and that thermal shift has the flatfish moving like they mean business.

The Meadowbrook Bridge has been the epicenter of the action, with boats stacked three deep on the southeast side working the 18- to 22-foot zone. I've been hitting it hard on the last three hours of incoming, and the fish are responding to white bucktails tipped with fresh smelt. Skip the squid strips — these fluke want the real deal. A 3/4-ounce white bucktail with a 4-inch smelt hooked behind the head through both lips is deadly. Add a teaser bucktail 18 inches up the line, same setup.

The bite window is narrow but productive. Start your drift tight to the bridge pilings and work southeast toward the channel edge. I'm seeing consistent action from guys who stay patient and work the bottom methodically. Lift and drop, lift and drop — don't just drag it. These fish want movement, but they're not chasing anything that's racing by.

Inside the inlet proper, the area around the Coast Guard station has been giving up keeper-class fish to boats working live peanut bunker on fishfinder rigs. The key is positioning yourself in that 25- to 30-foot sweet spot where the channel starts to shallow up. The current has been moderate on this moon phase, making it fishable without getting your sinker dragged all over creation.

What's driving this bite is simple: bait concentration. The warmer bay water is pulling massive schools of spearing and juvenile bunker through the inlet on every tide change. I watched clouds of bait getting pushed around the jetties yesterday morning, and where there's bait, there's fluke. The fish are staging in the deeper holes, ambushing whatever gets swept their way.

The ocean side has been tougher, but don't write it off completely. Early morning trips to the 40-foot line south of the inlet have produced scattered fish for boats willing to cover water. Diamond jigs in white and chartreuse are taking fish, but you need to work them aggressively. These aren't the lazy bay fish — ocean fluke want speed and flash.

Weakfish are making their presence known too, which is something I haven't been able to say with confidence in years. Small schools are moving through the inlet on the flood tide, mostly at night. Guys fishing the channel edges with bucktails after sunset are picking up fish in the 14- to 18-inch range. It's not a blitz, but it's consistent enough to get excited about.

The bass situation remains frustrating. Scattered fish are around, but nothing you can count on. A few boats working the inlet mouth at first light have connected with schoolies on small metals, but it's more hope than strategy at this point. The bunker schools haven't really organized yet, and until they do, the bass fishing will stay spotty.

Looking ahead, this weekend's new moon should amp up the tidal flow and really get things moving. I'm expecting the fluke bite to spread out from the Meadowbrook area as more fish move into feeding position. The key will be finding the bait concentrations — where you see diving birds and nervous water, that's where you want to be.

Water clarity has been decent despite some afternoon thunderstorms, and the salinity gradient between bay and ocean water is creating perfect ambush zones for predators. If you're planning to fish this weekend, focus on the tide changes and don't be afraid to move if the action dies. These fish are mobile right now, and the successful anglers are the ones willing to chase them.

reports.headline: Captree drift fires as bay water warms — fluke to 6 pounds on bucktails
reports.subhead: Mixed bags of sea bass, porgies, and ling round out the action as June heat kicks in.
reports.body_markdown:
The bay finally feels like June. Water temps hit 68 degrees this week, and you can feel the difference in everything from the bait movement to how aggressive the fish are feeding. The Captree fleet has been crushing it on the ocean side, with fluke up to 6 pounds coming over the rails on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and chartreuse bucktails.

The Robert Moses bridge drift has been the money spot for keeper fluke. I've been working 25 to 35 feet of water on the outgoing tide, dragging 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with 5-inch white Gulp. The key is keeping contact with bottom but not anchoring your jig — let it bounce and hop with the current. The bigger fish are holding in the deeper pockets near the bridge pilings, so don't be afraid to work tight to structure.

What's really impressive is the mixed bag action. While you're targeting fluke, you're picking up quality sea bass, fat porgies, and some surprising ling. The sea bass bite has been particularly strong — limits are common on diamond jigs and high-low rigs with clam strips. I watched one angler switch from bucktails to clams after limiting out on sea bass and immediately start hooking ling in the 3 to 5 pound range.

The ocean structure has been producing better quality fish than the bay this week. The warming water is pulling bait offshore, and the fluke are following. I'm seeing boats work the 40 to 50 foot depths south of the inlet with consistent action. Sabitiki rigs are deadly for the sea bass when they're stacked up, and I've seen guys pull three at a time.

Bait presentation matters more as the water warms. The fish are getting pickier, so fresh bait is crucial. Squid strips on the bucktails are outfishing old bait, and if you can get fresh spearing or peanut bunker, live-line them near structure on fishfinder rigs. The current has been moderate — perfect for controlling your drift without fighting it.

Night fishing has started to turn on for stripers in the bay. I'm hearing reports of slot fish on clam bellies around the bridges and channel edges. The key is fishing the moving water — incoming tide pushes bait through the inlet, and the bass stage up to ambush. Bass Assassins and soft plastics are working when the clam bite slows down.

The new moon is Friday, which means spring tides and strong current flow. This should flush more bait out of the bay and concentrate fish at the inlet mouth. I'm watching for the evening drain — that's when the weakfish typically show up for their first real push of the season. The water temperature gradient between bay and ocean is setting up perfectly for it.

Looking ahead, this warming trend should continue the fluke bite and start bringing the summer species inshore. The porgies are already thick, and I expect the sea bass action to stay strong through the weekend. If you're planning to fish, focus on the ocean side structure during the day and the bay edges at night. The fish are there — you just need to put your bait where they're feeding.

reports.headline: Moriches Bay fluke fishing fires as thermal layers stack bait in the shallows
reports.subhead: Doormat summer flounder to 7 pounds crushing bucktails in 6 feet as bay temps climb past ocean water.
reports.body_markdown:
The thermal engine that drives Moriches Bay is hitting full stride, and the fluke fishing is responding exactly like the physics predict. Bay water pushed past 74 degrees this week while the ocean side of the inlet held at 68 — that 6-degree gradient is creating a conveyor belt of bait that's stacking summer flounder in the skinny water like I haven't seen since early July last season.

The action is concentrated in that magic 4-to-8-foot zone where the bay's shallow structure meets the deeper channels. I'm talking about the edges off Tuthill Point, the drop-offs along the Westhampton flats, and especially that sweet spot where the east-west channel curves toward Smith Point. The fish are sitting right on those transitions, ambushing spearing and juvenile bunker that are getting pushed around by the thermal layers.

Tactics are all about finesse in this skinny water. I'm running 1/4-ounce bucktails — anything heavier and you're bouncing bottom too hard in 6 feet of water. White and chartreuse combinations are producing, tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets in pearl or nuclear chicken. The key is the drift speed — you need that Minn Kota to slow you down when the wind tries to push you too fast across the structure.

The quality has been exceptional. Multiple fish in the 5-to-7-pound range this week, with several pushing that magical doormat threshold. These aren't the skinny spring fish — these are thick, post-spawn females that have been feeding hard on the abundant bait. The 20-inch minimum is actually helping here; we're seeing more fish in that 19-to-22-inch slot that would have been kept under the old regs, and they're growing into real quality.

What's driving this bite is the bait concentration. The thermal stratification in the bay is creating these invisible walls that funnel spearing and juvenile bunker into predictable areas. When you find that 2-degree temperature break on your fish finder, that's where the food chain stacks up. The fluke know it, and they're positioning accordingly.

Tide timing matters more than usual right now. The outgoing has been the producer, especially that last two hours before low water. The ebb pulls cooler, oxygen-rich water from the deeper channels across the flats, and it carries scent trails that draw the fluke up from their holding spots. I'm seeing the best action from 7 AM to 10 AM on the morning ebb, then again from 6 PM to sunset on the evening drop.

The inlet itself has been productive for mixed bags. Striped bass in the 24-to-32-inch range are working the rips on the flood tide, hitting 6-inch Hogy soft plastics and live peanut bunker. The bass fishing isn't spectacular, but it's consistent — perfect for filling out a fluke trip when the flatfish bite slows.

Porgies are thick on the deeper structure around the inlet mouth. The 15-to-20-foot humps are loaded with keeper-sized fish, and they're aggressive on small bucktails tipped with clam or squid strips. It's a good backup plan when the fluke get finicky in the afternoon heat.

Looking ahead, this thermal pattern should hold through the weekend. The new moon on Friday means moderate tides — not the ripping currents that can scatter bait, but enough water movement to keep oxygen levels up and fish active. I'm expecting the skinny water bite to stay strong, especially if we get some cloud cover to break up the intense sun that's been hammering the shallows by midday.

The real test comes next week when we're forecast to hit the mid-80s air temps. If bay water climbs past 78 degrees, we might see the fluke push to the deeper edges or become more nocturnal. But for now, this is prime time for Moriches Bay summer flounder — the kind of fishing that makes you remember why you fell in love with this dynamic system in the first place.

reports.headline: Bass blitz the inlet as bay water hits 68 degrees
reports.subhead: Outgoing tides after dark are producing keeper stripers on live bunker and plugs.
reports.body_markdown:
The night bite is absolutely on fire right now. Bay water finally cracked 68 degrees this week, and that thermal gradient between the cooler ocean and warmer bay is stacking bait on every flood tide and holding bass on the ebb. I've been working the inlet from sunset to midnight, and the action has been consistent enough to set your watch by.

Best fishing starts about an hour into the outgoing tide when the bay starts draining hard. Bass are staging just outside the inlet mouth in 25 to 30 feet, ambushing peanut bunker and spearing getting swept out on the current. Live-lined peanuts on a simple fishfinder rig are absolutely deadly — 3/0 circle hook, 30-pound fluorocarbon leader, just enough weight to get down in the current. Let the bait swim naturally in the flow, and when a bass picks it up, count to three before setting the hook.

Plugs are working just as well for guys who prefer artificials. Swimming plugs like the Bomber Long A in bunker patterns, worked slow and steady through the current breaks, are getting crushed. The key is staying tight to the structure — those bass are hugging the jetty rocks and the channel edges where the current creates eddies and confusion.

Sizes have been impressive. Most fish are running 24 to 32 inches, with a few pushing the 36-inch mark. Had one angler show me photos of a 38-incher he released Tuesday night on a live bunker. The fish are fat and healthy, clearly feeding well on the abundant bait.

Fluke fishing in the bay has been solid during daylight hours. The Ponquogue Bridge area is producing steady action on the drift with bucktails and Gulp. White and chartreuse 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with 4-inch Swimming Mullets are the go-to rig. Fish the deeper holes on either side of the bridge in 20 to 25 feet. The current flow under the bridge creates a natural feeding lane, and fluke are positioned along the edges waiting for bait to get swept through.

Weakfish are starting to show up in their traditional spots. The canal area has been producing a few nice ones on the evening tides. Small bucktails with pink or white teasers, bounced along the bottom in 12 to 15 feet, are getting picked up. These fish are spooky, so light tackle and quiet presentations are essential.

Bait situation is excellent. Peanut bunker are thick throughout the bay, especially around the deeper channels near Hampton Bays. Spearing are schooled up tight to the docks and bulkheads. For those throwing nets, early morning and late evening are prime times when the bait moves shallow.

Water clarity has been good despite some afternoon thunderstorms. The bay is running clean with good visibility, which is helping the fluke bite during daylight hours. Ocean side is slightly off-color from recent weather, but not enough to shut down the inlet fishing.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon this weekend, which means spring tides and stronger current flow. That should really fire up the inlet fishing as more bait gets pushed around. The forecast shows lighter winds through the weekend, so conditions should be prime for both day and night fishing.

The weakfish bite should continue to improve as we move deeper into June. These fish typically show up in better numbers as water temperatures stabilize in the upper 60s. Keep an eye on the Tiana Beach area as well — that's been a sleeper spot for weakfish in years past.

For night fishing the inlet, remember to bring a good spotlight and know your way around in the dark. The jetties can be treacherous, and boat traffic picks up on weekends even after sunset. Fish smart, fish safe, and you'll be rewarded with some of the best striper fishing Shinnecock has to offer.

reports.headline: Southwest Ledge bass bite heats up as bay water climbs past 65 degrees
reports.subhead: Trophy stripers staging on the thermal breaks while fluke fishing explodes in the shallows.
reports.body_markdown:
The water's finally talking our language out here. Bay temperatures pushed past 65 degrees this week, and that's the magic number that gets everything moving around Block Island. The Southwest Ledge has been absolutely electric for striped bass, with fish to 38 pounds coming over the rail on live peanut bunker and fresh mackerel chunks.

I've been working the 40 to 60-foot contours where the cooler ocean water meets that warming bay flow, and the bass are stacked up on these thermal breaks like they're waiting in line. The key has been finding that temperature gradient — sometimes it's a razor-thin 2-degree difference that holds all the fish. Live-lining peanut bunker on a fishfinder rig with a 6/0 circle hook has been deadly, especially on the incoming tide when the bait gets pushed up against the ledge structure.

The fluke bite has absolutely exploded in the shallows around the island. We're seeing doormat-class fish in 15 to 25 feet of water, which is unusual for this early in June. A 7-pound, 3-ounce fluke came up yesterday on a white 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet rigged on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, drifted slow over the sandy bottom north of the harbor. The key is keeping your bait just kissing the bottom — these fish are aggressive but they want that natural presentation.

What's really interesting is how the wind farm area has been producing. The structure around those turbines has created an artificial reef system that's holding bait and attracting sea bass in numbers I haven't seen in years. We're talking keeper-sized fish on every drop, with green crabs and clam strips on high-low rigs doing the damage in 80 to 100 feet of water. The blackfish action around the turbine bases has been solid too, though you need to get your baits right into the structure to connect.

The porgies have been thick around the deeper wrecks and rocky bottom, but they're running smaller than usual. Still, they're great table fare and perfect for keeping the kids busy while you wait for the bigger fish to show. Small pieces of clam or squid on size 4 hooks are all you need.

Bait availability has been outstanding. The peanut bunker schools are thick from the harbor mouth all the way out to the ledge, and the sand eels are starting to group up in the deeper water. I've been seeing more mackerel than usual for this time of year, which explains why the bass bite has been so consistent. When you've got that much natural forage around, the fish settle into predictable feeding patterns.

The moon phase is working in our favor too. We're coming off a new moon, so the tides aren't as extreme, but there's still enough current to move bait and trigger feeding. The outgoing tide has been the most productive, especially that last two hours before slack water when everything gets concentrated in the deeper channels.

Water clarity has been exceptional — that gin-clear Block Island water that makes this place special. Visibility is running 15 to 20 feet in most spots, which means you need to scale down your leaders and be more careful with your presentations. I've been using 20-pound fluorocarbon leaders instead of my usual 30, and it's made a noticeable difference in the number of bites.

Looking ahead, this weekend's weather looks perfect for getting out there. Light southwest winds and calm seas should make for ideal conditions, especially for targeting those trophy bass on the ledge. The full moon is still a week away, so we won't have those big spring tides yet, but the fishing should remain consistent.

The real story here is that Block Island is hitting its summer stride right on schedule. The water temperatures, bait concentrations, and fish behavior are all aligning perfectly. This is what we wait for all winter — when the island becomes the striped bass capital of the East Coast. Get out there while the bite is hot.

reports.headline: Diamond jigs fire at the Point as bass push bait against the boulder fields
reports.subhead: Keeper stripers to 26 pounds hitting metals on the south side while fluke action stays steady in 30 feet.
reports.body_markdown:
The Point is doing what it does best right now — concentrating bass against structure and giving diamond jig fishermen the kind of action that makes this place legendary. The south side boulder fields have been producing keeper stripers consistently, with fish pushing into the 20-pound class and beyond. One charter this week brought 15 bass to the boat with five going over 18 pounds, topped by a 26-pounder that hit a diamond jig in the classic Montauk fashion.

The key has been working the jigs vertically along the boulder edges where the current sweeps bait against the rocks. These aren't your typical schoolie bass — most of the fish coming up are clear keepers, with plenty in the 31-inch-plus range. The diamond jigs are outproducing everything else because they get down fast in the current and trigger that aggressive response when bass are feeding on sand eels and small bunker pushed tight to structure.

Fluke fishing has been the steady producer for those looking to fill the cooler. The south side drops in 25 to 35 feet have been holding good numbers, with keepers mixed in among the shorts. White Gulp swimming mullets on bucktails continue to be the go-to rig, though you need to work them slow on the drift. The better fish — including some pushing 5 pounds — are coming on the longer drifts where you can keep the bait in the strike zone.

Sea bass are showing up as a bonus on the fluke grounds, with some nice 17-inch fish coming over the rail. The structure south of the lighthouse has been particularly productive, especially on the incoming tide when bait gets pushed up against the rocks.

Water conditions have been prime for this kind of fishing. The south side has been fishable most days, with that gentle 2-foot swell that lets you work structure properly without getting beat up. The key is timing your trips around the tide — the last hour of the ebb and first two hours of the flood have been the most productive windows.

The bait situation is what's driving this action. Sand eels are thick around the Point, and when the current pushes them against the boulder fields, the bass stack up to ambush them. That's why the diamond jigs are so effective — they mimic those sand eels perfectly when worked vertically along the structure.

Looking ahead, we're moving into the heart of summer fishing at Montauk. The full moon this weekend should fire up the tides even more, which typically means better current flow around the Point and more aggressive feeding. I'll be watching for the classic Montauk pattern — bass feeding hard on the moving water, especially during those prime tide changes at dawn and dusk. The south side should remain the focus, but don't sleep on the north side if the wind allows. When conditions line up right at the Point, there's no place like it on the East Coast.

reports.headline: Porgy bonanza fires up Shelter Island as bay water hits prime temps
reports.subhead: Jumbo scup stack thick on the flood while weakfish push into the shallows.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic Bay porgy bite has exploded into full summer mode, with jumbo scup stacked thick around Shelter Island and the Middle Grounds producing limits of 2- to 3-pound fish for anyone willing to work a proper chum slick. Water temps have climbed into the mid-60s — that magic number that fires up the bay's legendary porgy population and pulls them into their classic summer feeding pattern.

The action has been most consistent on the flood tide, particularly the first two hours as water pushes through the channels around Jessup's Neck and spreads across the flats. I've been anchoring in 25 to 30 feet, laying down a steady chum line of crushed clams, and watching the fish stack up like cordwood. The key is patience — give that chum 10 minutes to work, then drop your rigs into the slick. Fresh clam strips on high-low rigs with 2/0 hooks are producing the best fish, though the jumbos seem to prefer whole littlenecks when you can keep the shorts off them.

Size has been impressive this week. Most keepers are running 16 to 18 inches, with plenty of fish pushing 19 inches and better. The real monsters — those 3-pound-plus doormat scup that make the Peconics famous — are showing up consistently in the deeper holes near Shelter Island's north shore. These fish require a different approach: heavier sinkers to hold bottom in the current, and the discipline to let them take the bait instead of rushing the hookset.

Weakfish have been the surprise bonus of the week. The warming bay water has pulled them out of their deeper haunts and scattered them across the flats from Noyack to Orient. Most are running 18 to 22 inches — solid keepers that fight like demons in the shallow water. They're hitting bucktails tipped with squid strips, worked slow along the bottom on the drift. The bite has been best early morning and late afternoon, when the light is low and the fish move up to feed.

The striped bass bite remains frustratingly inconsistent. A few slot fish are showing up around Orient Point, particularly on the rips during moving water, but nothing like the reliable spring run we expect. Water temps in the Sound are still running cooler than the bay — that thermal barrier is keeping the main body of fish from pushing through Plum Gut in numbers. The bass that are here seem to be residents, fish that winter in the deeper holes and spread out as conditions warm.

Bait has been the story this week. The bay is alive with spearing and juvenile bunker, particularly in the shallows around Three Mile Harbor and Sag Harbor Cove. This forage base is what's driving the porgy bite and pulling the weakfish shallow. The abundance of small bait also explains why the bluefish action has been spotty — when there's this much natural food around, the blues don't need to chase artificials with the same aggression.

Current has been moderate with the quarter moon phase, making for comfortable fishing conditions but requiring some adjustment in technique. The gentler flow means chum disperses more slowly, so you need to be more generous with your slick to draw fish from a distance. It also means lighter sinkers will hold bottom, allowing for more natural bait presentation.

Looking ahead, the approaching new moon should intensify the bite across all species. New moon tides will flush more bait through the system and concentrate fish on the structure. The porgy bite should remain strong through the month as water temps stabilize in the upper 60s. For weakfish, watch for the evening bite to improve as longer days push feeding activity later into the night. The real prize will be if this new moon cycle finally triggers the main striper migration through Plum Gut — conditions are setting up perfectly for that classic June push that makes the Peconic system legendary.

reports.headline: Orient Point rips fire as bunker schools push through Plum Gut
reports.subhead: Bass to 35 pounds crash bait pods while porgy action heats up the oyster cages.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty years walking these beaches, and I still get that tingle when the water starts talking. This week, she's been downright chatty.

The big news is Orient Point. Tuesday morning, just after slack water turned to flood, I watched the most beautiful thing — acres of bunker getting pushed through Plum Gut like someone was herding cattle. Bass were underneath them, rolling and slashing, some real cows in the mix. Tommy Kowalski put his nephew on a 35-pounder that morning, fish took a live bunker on a circle hook right in the white water where the rip meets the point. Kid fought it for twenty minutes before Tommy could get the net under her.

The key is timing the tide change. You want to be set up on the west side of the point as the flood starts pushing. Those bunker schools get compressed against the rocks, and the bass know it. I've been running 6-inch live bunker on fishfinder rigs, 6/0 circles, 30-pound leader. Let the current do the work — no need to get fancy when the fish are that aggressive.

Further west along my beat, the oyster cages off Rocky Point have been holding decent porgy. Nothing huge — mostly 12 to 14 inches — but steady picking if you can deal with the current. Green crabs on high-low rigs, size 4 hooks. The trick is anchoring uptide of the cages and letting your rig swing down into the structure. Water's been running clean, maybe 8 to 10 feet of visibility, which has the porgy feeding confident.

Horton Point's been giving up some nice bluefish in the evenings. Cocktail blues mostly, 3 to 5 pounds, but they're thick when the tide's moving. Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks work fine, but I've had better luck with small poppers right at sunset. Something about that surface commotion when the light's fading — gets them fired up.

Water temperature's been climbing steady. Hit 64 degrees at Orient Point yesterday, which is right where it should be for mid-June. That's warm enough to pull the weakfish up from deeper water, and I'm starting to see signs. Found some small pods of grass shrimp in the shallows off Mattituck Inlet Tuesday evening, which usually means the weaks aren't far behind. Haven't connected yet, but I'm watching.

The bait situation tells the whole story. Besides those bunker schools moving through the Gut, I'm seeing good numbers of spearing along the rocky shoreline and sand eels in the deeper pockets. The spearing are what's keeping the smaller bass around — 20 to 28 inch fish that are perfect for the table. Small Clouser Minnows on light spinning gear, or just a size 2 hook with a piece of spearing if you want to keep it simple.

Moon's waxing toward full this weekend, which should push more bait through the system. Spring tides always stir things up, especially in Plum Gut where the current can really rip. I'm planning to be at Orient Point Saturday morning, early flood tide, with a cooler full of fresh bunker. If this pattern holds, it could be the start of something special.

One thing I've learned in six decades out here — when the water's this clean and the bait's moving like this, you don't overthink it. Keep your tackle simple, watch the tide, and let the fish tell you what they want. Right now, they're saying bunker and they're saying Orient Point. I'd listen if I were you.

reports.headline: Race rips fire as 52-degree water triggers bass blitz in eastern Sound
reports.subhead: Plum Gut and The Race delivering slot fish on bucktails as water temps hit the magic number.
reports.body_markdown:
The eastern Sound just flipped the switch. Water temps climbed from 50 to 52 degrees this week, and that two-degree jump changed everything. The Race is absolutely firing, and Plum Gut is producing consistent action on both flood and ebb tides.

I've been hammering The Race on the ebb current, working 3/4-ounce bucktails in white and chartreuse through the deep water where the current screams at 4 knots. The key is getting your jig down fast in that 100-foot zone before the rip grabs it. I'm running 30-pound braid straight to a 40-pound fluoro leader, no swivel — you need that direct connection when these fish hit in the current.

The bass are stacked in the eddies behind the main rip line. You'll see the surface boil, but the real action is 80 to 100 feet down where the current breaks over the bottom structure. I've been putting fish in the boat almost every drift when the tide's moving hard. Slot fish from 28 to 32 inches, with a few overs mixed in that go back.

Plum Gut is equally productive but requires different timing. The flood tide has been the money shot, especially the first two hours when the current builds from slack. I'm fishing the same bucktail setup but working shallower water, 40 to 60 feet. The bass are ambushing bait getting swept through the gut, so you want your jig bouncing bottom on a tight line.

What's driving this bite is simple — baitfish are moving with the warming water. Spearing are thick along the Orient Point shoreline, and I'm seeing peanut bunker getting flushed through both the Gut and The Race on the tide changes. The bass know it and they're positioned to feed.

The 52-degree mark seems to be the trigger point. Below 50, these fish were sluggish and scattered. Above 52, they're aggressive and predictable. I'm reading 52 to 53 degrees consistently now from Orient Point west to Fishers Island, with slightly cooler water on the Connecticut side.

Technique matters in this current. At The Race, I'm using a three-way rig with a 6-ounce bank sinker to hold bottom, then running an 18-inch leader to the bucktail. Let it bounce and sweep with the current — don't fight the drift. At Plum Gut, I'm power-drifting with the engine, bumping in and out of gear to control the presentation.

Bluefish are also in the mix, especially at The Race. Big gorilla blues that will test your drag and steal your bucktails if you're not careful. They're hitting the same jigs as the bass, so be ready for anything when that rod loads up.

Weakfish are starting to show in the deeper water off Fishers Island. Nothing consistent yet, but I'm marking fish on the finder in 60 to 80 feet. The full moon this Friday should trigger some serious tide movement — spring tides always get the bait moving and the predators feeding.

Looking ahead, this warming trend should continue the bite through the weekend. I'm watching for water temps to push toward 55 degrees, which typically brings the first real bunker schools into the Sound. When that happens, the surface action will explode. Until then, it's all about working the bottom with bucktails and reading the current.

reports.headline: Bass crash the Norwalk rocks as bait pods stack on spring tide surge
reports.subhead: Schoolies to 32 inches hitting bucktails and soft plastics in the wash around the islands.
reports.body_markdown:
The spring tide surge that peaked Tuesday night did exactly what I expected — it flushed massive bait pods out of the harbors and stacked them against the rocky structure around the Norwalk Islands. By Wednesday morning, the bass were all over it.

I've been watching this pattern develop for two weeks now. Water temps finally hit that magic 68-degree mark in the shallows, and the spearing have been thick along the Connecticut shoreline from Stamford to New Haven. When you get spring tides moving that much bait around structure, the bass can't resist.

The action has been best on the back side of the islands where the current creates those perfect eddies. I'm talking about the rocky points on Sheffield and Chimon islands specifically. Fish are holding in 12 to 20 feet, right where the current breaks around the boulders. White and chartreuse 3/4-ounce bucktails with 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets have been deadly. Cast uptide and let it swing through the rocks — that's when they hammer it.

The bite window has been narrow but intense. First light to about 8 AM, then again from 6 PM to dark. During the day, you need to work deeper — out to the 30-foot contour where the thermocline is setting up. The fish are there, but they're more finicky. Switch to lighter jigs, maybe 1/2-ounce, and work them slower.

Port Jefferson has been producing too, especially around the ferry terminal pilings on the incoming tide. The structure there creates the same kind of current breaks that hold bait. I've been hearing about keeper fluke mixed in with the bass action — nothing huge, but solid 18 to 20-inch fish on the sandy patches between the rocks.

What's got me really excited is the bait situation. The spearing schools are getting thicker every day, and I'm starting to see some adult bunker moving through. That's early for bunker, but the water temps are running about two degrees warmer than normal for mid-June. When those bunker schools really establish, that's when the big bass show up.

The Stratford Shoal area has been hit or miss. The rip is running hard with these spring tides — maybe too hard for consistent fishing. But when you time it right, around the tide changes, there are fish there. Bigger fish too. I heard about a couple of 30-plus-inch bass coming off the shoal this week, but you need to be able to handle the current.

Porgies have been a pleasant surprise. The Middle Ground Light area has been loaded with them — big ones, 12 to 14 inches. They're in 25 to 35 feet, and they're hungry. Small hooks, size 6 or 8, with pieces of clam or squid. It's been a great backup when the bass bite slows down.

Looking ahead, we're moving into neap tides this weekend, which should calm things down and let the fish settle into more predictable patterns. The full moon is still a week away, so we've got some stable conditions coming. I'm watching for the water temps to push into the low 70s — that's when the summer pattern really kicks in and the fish spread out more.

The key right now is mobility. Don't get stuck on one spot. The bait is moving with these tides, and the fish are following. Keep your eyes open for bird activity and surface disturbances. When you see the terns diving, get there fast. This bite won't last forever, but while it's on, it's as good as it gets in the central Sound.

reports.headline: Bass stack on Execution Rocks as bunker schools finally push west into the Sound
reports.subhead: Slot fish hitting live peanuts and bucktails as water temps climb past the magic 66-degree mark.
reports.body_markdown:
After weeks of waiting for the bait to show, the western Sound finally came alive this week. Water temps hit 66 degrees in the bays — a solid four degrees warmer than the ocean side — and that thermal gradient is doing exactly what it's supposed to do: stacking bait on the flood and holding bass on the ebb.

The bunker schools that have been teasing us all spring finally pushed west past Matinecock Point, and the bass followed like they had dinner reservations. I'm seeing good action from Execution Rocks all the way down to the Stepping Stones, with the best bite coming on the outgoing tide when that warmer bay water drains out and creates a feeding highway.

Live peanut bunker is the ticket right now — hook them through the back, fish them on a fishfinder rig tight to structure, and hang on. The bass are averaging 28 to 35 inches, with a few overs mixed in. One guy I talked to at the dock pulled a 40-incher off the rocks Tuesday morning, released it clean. These fish are loaded with eggs still, which tells me the spawn isn't completely finished despite what the calendar says.

If you can't get live bait, white bucktails with chartreuse teasers are producing. Three-quarter ounce heads seem to be the sweet spot — heavy enough to get down in the current but light enough to work with some action. Drag them slow along the bottom on the drift, especially around the channel edges where the current breaks.

The Throgs Neck Bridge pilings are holding fish too, but you need to time it right. Hit them on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current really starts to rip. The bass are using those pilings as ambush points, waiting for bait to get swept past. Live eels work great here if you can get them, but bucktails will do the job.

Fluke fishing has been spotty at best. The water's still a bit cool for them to really turn on, and frankly, there's not much bait in the traditional fluke spots yet. I'm marking some fish in 25 to 30 feet off Lloyd Neck, but they're mostly shorts. The few keepers coming up are hitting white Gulp on the drift, but it's a grind.

Porgies are thick around any structure in 15 to 25 feet. Clam strips on high-low rigs will fill the cooler fast. Nothing fancy needed — just find the rocks and drop down. The Stepping Stones area has been particularly good for keeper-sized porgies.

The moon's been working in our favor too. We just came off new moon spring tides, which really got the water moving and flushed a lot of bait out of the back bays. That's what finally triggered this bunker movement. Now we're building toward the full moon on the 19th, which should keep the current strong and the fish active.

Looking ahead, I'm watching for the water to hit 68 degrees consistently. That's when the fluke really wake up and start feeding aggressively. The way the temps are climbing, we should be there by next week. The bass bite should stay strong as long as the bunker stick around — and with water this warm in the bays, I don't see them leaving anytime soon.

One thing to watch: the weekend boat traffic is getting heavy. If you're going to fish the popular spots like Execution Rocks or the bridge, get there early or stay late. The fish don't like the parade of boats any more than we do.

reports.headline: Mid-June transition catches Jersey beat between data gaps and bait shifts
reports.subhead: With primary offshore buoys offline and SST package two days stale, the Shore plays the calendar — Raritan winding down, ocean structure waking up.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest lead today is that the analyst desk is flying with one engine. Buoy 44025 — the workhorse New York Bight reference twelve miles south of Islip and the station every Jersey captain cross-checks against Ambrose — is offline. Block Island's 44097 water temperature feed is intermittent and not giving a clean number. The latest published SST composite in the catalog is dated June 10, two days behind today's water. That means no defensible single-degree Fahrenheit reading I'm willing to print for the Hook or the Manasquan Ridge this morning. What I can say with confidence is what the calendar and the last clean SST frame told us: by the second week of June the Raritan complex is typically running in the mid-to-upper 60s, the nearshore ocean from Sea Girt to Barnegat is climbing through the low 60s, and Cape May's rips are already pushing 65. Without fresh buoy confirmation, treat those as bracketing assumptions, not gospel.

What that thermal bracket means for the beat is straightforward. The Raritan Bay spring striper show — the bunker-and-bass circus that defined April and May from the Reach Channel down to the Keansburg flats — is in its closing chapter. Once the bay pushes past 66, the big resident females slide out around the Hook and start working the three-mile line and the Shrewsbury Rocks on cooler ocean water. The Hook rips on the outgoing, particularly the back side of the ebb when the rip stacks against the southerly breeze, is where I'd be spending dawns this week. Inside the inlets, Manasquan and Shark River are squarely in fluke mode now, and the ocean fluke grounds from the Axel Carlson down through Barnegat Ridge should be holding fish on the drift in 40 to 55 feet.

The on-the-ground picture, synthesized from a quiet overnight intel cycle, is one of transition rather than a single dominant pattern. Bunker schools are still tractoring through the bay but the bass column on them is thinning and the fish that remain are increasingly post-spawn and lean — the trophy class is moving. Sea bass season is open and the wrecks and reef pieces from 17 Fathoms inshore to the Axel Carlson are the highest-percentage bottom trip on the board right now, with sand eels showing in the column and jigs outperforming clams when you mark fish stacked above the structure. Fluke reports out of Shark River and the Manasquan back have been steady on short-to-keeper ratios that favor patience — outgoing tide, bucktail-and-Gulp, the deeper holes off the railroad bridge.

Down the southern end of the beat, Cape May and the Delaware rips are the sleeper play. When the northern bays warm past comfort, the rips off Cape May Point and the mouth of the Delaware become the most reliable striper structure on the Jersey coast through late June — moving water, tide-line bait, and slot fish that will eat a bucktail or a live spot. Weakfish should also be a real conversation in Delaware Bay and the Great Bay sedges right now; the back-bay grass edges on the top of the incoming with a pink shad or a small swimmer is the classic play, and the second week of June is historically when the better tiderunners show.

Looking three to five days out, the controlling variable is wind. A sustained southerly stacks warm surface water against the Jersey beach and accelerates the inside-bay thermal exit — meaning the Raritan window closes faster. A northeast pulse, even a modest one, drags cooler slope water shoreward and can re-set the inlet bite for another week. I want eyes on Sandy Hook's tide-gauge water temperature trend and the first clean 44025 reading whenever NDBC brings it back online; a jump through 68 inside the bay is the trigger to abandon the Reach and commit to the Hook rips and the Shrewsbury Rocks full-time. New moon is not in play this week, so tide ranges are moderate — favor the inlets on the back half of the ebb rather than the slack-water windows.

The call for the next several tides: fluke the inlets and the 50-foot ocean line on the drift, jig sea bass on the inshore wrecks before the July one-fish limit clamps down, work the Hook outgoing at first light for the last of the bay bass, and if you've got the fuel, the Cape May rips are the most underrated striper bite in the state right now. I'll have firmer numbers when the buoy array and the SST pipeline catch up.

reports.headline: Bay heats ahead of the ocean as June fluke and bass settle into Marine Parkway pattern
reports.subhead: With offshore buoy reference offline, the dominant signal is the inside-outside thermal split driving bait and predators into Rockaway Inlet on the moving tides.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk is running thin today. The 44025 array off Long Island is offline, taking out our primary offshore reference, and 44097 up at Block Island has been intermittent on water temperature. No fresh SST package has dropped since June 10. That means the read on Jamaica Bay this morning has to be built from structure and season rather than a clean buoy line, and the honest answer is that we are in the middle of the early-summer inside-outside split — back-bay flats and marsh edges warming hard into the mid-60s under June sun while the open Atlantic off Rockaway Beach lags several degrees behind. That gradient, more than any single number, is what is steering fish right now.

What that thermal engine means for this beat is straightforward. The bay is the warm reservoir, the ocean is the cool sink, and Rockaway Inlet is the throat between them. Every outgoing tide pulls warmer, bait-rich water out past Breezy Point and dumps it into a cooler receiving body, and that is exactly the seam where striped bass stage. The Marine Parkway Bridge pilings remain the single most reliable piece of structure in the zone on the back half of the drop, with slot fish and a scattering of overslot holdovers working the down-current side of the towers in 18 to 30 feet.
