Fluke have spread from the deeper inlet channels onto the bayside flats and channel edges now that bay temps are committed to the 60s, and the first real porgy push should be setting up around the harder bottom near the bridge abutments and the channel edges off Canarsie Pier.

On the ground, the bass bite has been a tide-stage game more than a location game. The bridge is producing best on the last two hours of the outgoing into slack, with soft plastics on a half-ounce to one-ounce jighead outfishing bait for the schoolie-to-slot class, and bunker chunks still doing the work when a bigger fish wants to eat. Live bunker, where you can get it, is the move at first light along the Breezy Point rip and the deeper cuts inside the inlet. The chunk bite that defined late April and early May has thinned as the resident fish have shifted to chasing peanut bunker and spearing, and that is a normal June transition rather than a sign the bay is emptying.

Fluke reports out of the bay have been the usual June mix — plenty of shorts, sea robins on every other drift, and a legitimate keeper rate for anglers willing to work bucktail-and-teaser rigs on the moving water rather than dead-stick bait. The drifts along the channel edges south of the Cross Bay Bridge and the deeper water off the airport flats have been the most consistent, with the better fish coming on the stronger tide pushes. Weakfish are around in modest numbers — nothing like the banner mornings of a few seasons back, but enough yellowfins mixed into the fluke drifts and the evening bridge bite to tell you the bay is healthy. Bluefish presence has been spotty inside; the cleaner shots have come along the Rockaway Beach surf on the dawn tide when bait gets pinned against the bar.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variable is wind. A sustained southwest pattern in June piles warmer ocean water against the Rockaway beachfront and accelerates the inshore migration of bunker schools, which would light up the surf from Breezy east toward the jetty fields and bring bigger bass back into casting range from the sand. A hard easterly would do the opposite — push cold water against the beach, knock the surf bite back, and concentrate the action inside the inlet and at the bridge. With the new moon approaching, tide ranges will build through the week, which favors the bridge bass bite on the bigger outgoings and tends to scatter fluke off the tightest channel edges onto adjacent flats. Watch for the first serious peanut bunker showings in the back of the bay; that is the trigger that turns the evening weakfish bite from incidental into targetable.

The bay is doing in June what the bay does in June. The thermal gradient is the story, the inlet is the choke point, and the angler who fishes moving water on the right side of the bridge with the right size profile is going to catch. I would not overthink it this week — be on the Marine Parkway pilings for the last of the outgoing, have a bucktail rod rigged for the drift back, and keep an eye on the wind forecast for the first real southwest stretch.

reports.headline: Captree fleet rides a mixed-bag ocean as inlet bait stages for the summer flip
reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and the SST package stalled at June 10, the read on Fire Island leans on inside-bay thermal cues and ocean-side party-boat signal.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this beat — NDBC 44025 south of Fire Island — is sensor-dark again, and the satellite SST pipeline hasn't refreshed since June 10, so today's read leans harder than usual on the inside water and what the rails are bringing home. 44097 down at Block is also intermittent on temperature, which knocks out the second-best proxy for what's flowing past the inlet. What's left is the structural picture: a Great South Bay that, by mid-June, is running well ahead of the ocean thermally, an inlet flushing colder, denser ocean water in on every flood, and a bait column that's already split between sand eels and squid on the outside and bunker, spearing, and the first real push of snappers stacking inside. Wind has been workable, seas knockdown most mornings, and the fleet has been getting out clean.

That thermal split is the whole story right now. When the bay sits five to eight degrees warmer than the ocean — which is exactly where we should be in the second week of June with no recent blow to mix it — the inlet becomes a conveyor belt. Outgoing tide dumps warm, bait-rich bay water over the bar and the bass and blues set up on the edges of it; incoming brings cooler ocean water and the bottom fish — sea bass, porgies, ling, the last of the cod — pile onto structure just outside. That's the pattern the Captree open boats are running on, and it's why the ocean trips right now are producing the kind of mixed-bag rail you only see for a few weeks a year before the water homogenizes into full summer.

The ocean wrecks and rockpiles southeast of the inlet are the standout. Sea bass are stacked thick in 60 to 90 feet, with limits coming on hammered diamond jigs in the three- to five-ounce range and sabikis loading up three at a clip when you drop into a tight school. Porgies are mixed in heavier than usual for this early — a sign the bottom temps are climbing past that mid-50s threshold where they get aggressive. Ling and the odd cod are still being scraped off the deeper pieces, which tells me the colder ocean layer hasn't fully retreated yet. Chub mackerel showing on the boats is the other tell — that's a clean-water, cool-edge fish, and they don't hang around once the surface punches past 65.

Inside, the bass story has shifted hard off bait and onto plastics, and that shift tracks the water warming through the upper 50s into the low 60s. The clam-and-bunker-chunk crowd anchoring the channels is grinding through doggies to find a keeper; the guys drifting Bass Assassins, Hogys, and paddle tails through the Robert Moses bridge abutments and the deeper holes between markers are getting cleaner shots at slot fish and the occasional over. The night tide at Captree has been the most consistent window — slack to early outgoing, fishing the down-current side of the pilings. Fluke are in the inlet and along the bayside drop into the channel, but the class is still mixed and you're throwing back four or five shorts for every keeper. The Democrat Point rip and the sod banks toward Sore Thumb haven't fully turned on yet for the surf crowd, though the bait is there.

Looking out three to five days, the move is bunker. The body of adult menhaden that's been working the beaches from Jones east is going to keep pushing, and once a pod commits to the inlet on an outgoing, the bass game changes overnight from finesse plastics to live-lining and snagging. Watch the wind: a sustained southwest will stack bait on the Fire Island beach from Democrat to the lighthouse and light up the dawn surf bite; a hard southeast will muddy the inside and push the fluke fleet out to the ocean side of the bridges. With the new moon working in next week, expect the tides to rip harder through the inlet, which historically triggers the first real weakfish showings around the Captree flats and the channel edges off Babylon.

The ocean is doing what it should be doing in mid-June, and the inlet is the seam where it matters. I'd be on the Moses bridges at first light on the outgoing with a bag of soft plastics, and I'd have a jigging stick rigged and ready the moment a bunker pod shows on the sounder. The bottom fishing outside is as good as it gets all year right now — don't sleep on it waiting for the bass to get easy.

reports.headline: Jones Inlet runs blind as 44025 stays dark, but June pattern holds bay-side
reports.subhead: With the primary offshore buoy offline and SST imagery four days stale, the bite read leans on bay thermal structure and bait position rather than fresh numbers.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest lead today is what we don't have. NDBC 44025, the Long Island offshore reference 30 miles south of Fire Island, is offline — sensor array down — and 44097 up at Block Island is intermittent on water temperature. The most recent SST package in the catalog is dated June 10, two days stale, and overnight forum collection produced nothing new to triangulate against. That leaves us reading the inlet the way we used to before every boat had a tablet: by what the calendar says, what the last good data showed, and what the bait is doing on the dock walks.

For mid-June on this beat, the controlling variable is the thermal gradient between Hempstead Bay and the ocean side of Jones Inlet. The back is warming faster than the front — that is the seasonal default, and nothing in the available data argues against it. That gradient is the engine: warm bay water pushing out on the ebb stacks bait at the inlet mouth and along the east jetty rip, while cooler ocean water shoving in on the flood pins fluke against the sand transitions inside the inlet. Translated to where to point the boat: I'd be working the inlet mouth and the east jetty on the last two hours of outgoing for bass on the surface or just under, and drifting the channel edges from the Coast Guard Station back toward Demo Point on the flood for fluke. Bunker are the tell — if you see adult bunker schools getting pushed against the jetty rocks on the ebb, the bass class on them this week should be solid mid-slot fish with a real shot at an overslot.

The Sloop Channel and the deeper cuts behind Short Beach should be holding fluke on the moving water, with the better grade of fish — 19 inches and up — coming on bigger baits than most guys are willing to fish. Strip baits, smelt-and-squid combos on a white bucktail with a teaser, and live snappers if you can find them yet, though the snapper class is probably still too small to liveline this early. The Meadowbrook drift on the southeast side of the bridge has been the percentage play in recent seasons through June, and that pattern holds: outgoing tide, white bucktail, work the shadow line. Weakfish are the wild card I keep coming back to — the back-bay holes around Wantagh and the deeper pockets off Freeport have been giving up tide-runners to guys throwing small soft plastics on light jigheads at first light and last light, and that fishery is quietly rebuilding into something worth taking seriously.

Bluefish should be a factor any time you find bait pinned, particularly outside the inlet on the ebb. I haven't seen anything to suggest a true bunker blitz yet — that tends to firm up later in June into early July on this beat — but choppers in the 3-to-6-pound range are around and they'll wreck a topwater plug fished over the bar at the inlet mouth on the dropping tide. Porgies are in on the structure, and the bridge abutments from the Wantagh down to Meadowbrook are the easy meat for anyone bringing kids out. Blackfish season is closed but worth noting the structure is holding them well based on the late-fall pattern that carried through.

Looking ahead three to five days, the variable to watch is wind direction. A persistent southwest will keep the bay warm, keep the bait stacked, and keep the thermal engine running clean — that is the constructive scenario. A hard northeast shift, which has chewed up this beat repeatedly the last two seasons, kills the drift inside, dirties the inlet, and pushes the ocean fish off the beach. I'd also want 44025 back online before I take any offshore read seriously; until that sensor comes up, anyone running south of the inlet is doing it on feel. Moon is building toward full late in the week, which means stronger tides, faster drifts, heavier bucktails — go up two ounces from what worked last weekend.

Fish the bay on the warm side of the gradient, fish the inlet on the moving water, and don't trust any temperature number you can't source. The data is thin this week. The fish don't care.

reports.headline: Moriches Bay runs ahead of offshore as inlet thermal gradient sharpens
reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and 44097 intermittent, the bay-to-ocean temperature break at Moriches Inlet becomes the controlling variable for this week's bite.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference is dark this morning. NDBC 44025 — the Long Island buoy that normally anchors any honest read on South Shore ocean state — is offline, and 44097 off Block Island has been feeding intermittent water-temperature data through the last package cycle. The most recent SST composite in the catalog is dated June 10, two days stale, and the overnight fishing-report intake produced nothing fresh from the zone. That leaves us reasoning from the June 10 thermal field, the seasonal trajectory, and what the bay itself is doing under our feet. Mid-June on Moriches means the back bay is climbing fast — historically through the high 60s and brushing 70°F on a sunny afternoon outgoing — while the nearshore Atlantic outside Cupsogue typically lags by six to ten degrees this time of year. With no live buoy to pin a number to, treat the inside-outside delta as the dominant feature and fish it.

That gradient is the engine. Every ebb out of Moriches Inlet right now is dumping warmer, bait-rich bay water into a cooler ocean, and the seam sets up just outside the jetty tips and along the east rip toward Cupsogue. Bass stage on the ocean side of that seam and feed up-current into it. The slot-class fish — 28 to 31 inches — are the dominant class through the inlet on the dropping tide, with the occasional overslot working the deeper scour hole on the west side where the channel pinches to roughly 18 to 22 feet. Fluke are the other half of the program: the bay is in its skinny-water phase, three to ten feet over the sand edges from Tuthill Point east toward the inlet flats, and the drift discipline question is the same one it always is in June — are you slow enough to keep a jig on the bottom in clean water without dragging through the warm pockets the keepers won't sit in.

Inlet structure is doing what it does post-spring: the storm cuts from the winter have re-sorted the sand on the ocean side, and the bar configuration off Cupsogue is holding a sluice that fishes best on the last two hours of the drop and the first hour of the flood. Bucktails in the half-to-three-quarter-ounce range tipped with Gulp are the honest answer when the current is ripping; soft plastics on a quarter-ounce jighead take over on the slack and the early flood when bass slide up onto the flats to hunt spearing and peanut bunker. The Westhampton side of the bay, west of the inlet up toward the East Moriches channels, has been the more reliable fluke grid — edges of three to seven feet, sand-to-grass transitions — while the bigger ocean-grade fish are pulling through the inlet itself on tide changes.

Weakfish are the wildcard worth mentioning. With bay temperatures climbing into the high 60s, the deeper holes off Tuthill and the channel bends behind Smith Point are the textbook setup for a late-incoming-into-slack bite on small plastics fished slow. Porgies have settled onto the harder bottom inside the bay and along the inlet rockpiles; blackfish remain a structure-and-crab game on the jetty rocks but are secondary to the fluke and bass program right now.

Look-ahead through the weekend and into early next week hinges on two things. First, whether 44025 comes back online — without it, we are flying on bay thermometers and satellite composites, and any sudden southerly blow will rearrange the inlet bait picture faster than we can confirm it. Second, the moon is building toward the full on the 29th, but the current set of tides is moderate, which favors the technical drift fisherman over the brute-force bait soaker. If a south-southwest wind sets up for two consecutive days, expect the ocean side to warm a degree or two and the bass bite at the inlet mouth to pull a half-tide earlier as the thermal seam slides inshore.

I'd be at the inlet on the last of the drop with a bucktail and a backup spinning rod rigged light for plastics, and I'd be willing to run west into the skinny water the moment the current goes slack. The data picture is thinner than I'd like this week, but the mechanism is not in doubt: fish the temperature break, fish the tide that moves it, and let the bay's heat do the recruiting for you.

reports.headline: Shinnecock runs blind as buoys go dark, but June thermal math still favors the inlet
reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and the SST package stalled at June 10, the bite call leans on tide mechanics and seasonal water-column structure rather than fresh telemetry.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this stretch of the South Shore is dark this morning. NOAA buoy 44025, the Long Island station that anchors every honest report from Moriches to Montauk, has its sensor array offline, and 44097 down at Block Island is feeding intermittent water temperature only. The Dr. Fish analyst package itself has no live conditions to publish today, and the satellite SST catalog hasn't refreshed since June 10. That means no clean number to put on the inlet mouth, no shelf-edge gradient to map, and no overnight validation from the field. Reporting around a data gap is part of the job in June, when fog, biofouling, and maintenance windows routinely knock the offshore network down for days at a stretch. What we do know is structural: we are deep into the second week of June, the bay has been warming hard on every flood for two weeks, and the last published SST frames showed the inside water running meaningfully warmer than the ocean side of the inlet.

That inside-outside delta is the engine that matters for this beat right now. Shinnecock Bay in mid-June behaves like a shallow solar collector — Tiana flats, the back side of the barrier beach, and the broad shoals north of the Ponquogue Bridge pick up heat fast, and every outgoing tide flushes that warmer, bait-rich water through the inlet throat into cooler ocean. Bass stack on the ocean side of the jetties and in the rip behind the east jetty tip to ambush whatever the tide hands them: spearing, sand eels, the first real push of bay anchovy, and the small bunker that have been working the bay since late May. Without a buoy number I won't pretend to know the exact thermal break, but the seasonal math says the productive window is the back half of the ebb into the first of the flood, after dark, with the inlet doing the work for you.

The signal from the bay over the past two weeks has been consistent with that pattern. Slot-class bass have been the dominant night-tide class inside the inlet and along the rockpile on the ocean side, with trolled and swum plugs worked low and slow producing better than fast retrieves — a classic sign that the fish are sitting in the current seam rather than chasing through the column. Fluke have set up on the standard early-summer drifts: the channel edges off Ponquogue, the drop into the inlet on the last of the incoming, and the sand-to-grass transitions on the Tiana side. Quality has been better than quantity, with a healthy ratio of keepers to shorts on bucktail-and-Gulp rigs in eight to eighteen feet. Weakfish remain the wildcard at the Ponquogue Bridge pilings on the dusk tide change; the body of fish that showed in late May appears to still be in the system, and the bridge lights at slack-to-outgoing are the highest-percentage shot.

Porgy fishing in the Shinnecock Canal and on the hard bottom up toward the railroad bridge has filled in on schedule, and the canal itself is fishing as the conveyor belt it always is in June — bait moving with every lock cycle, bass and the occasional weakfish staging on the south end. Bluefish presence has been patchy rather than the wall of choppers we sometimes get this week, which tracks with a cooler-than-average ocean side holding them slightly offshore of the beach.

Looking three to five days out, the controlling variable is wind. Any sustained southwest at fifteen-plus will stack warm surface water against the beach and accelerate the inside-outside exchange on the ebb — that is when the inlet jaws get good in a hurry, particularly the two hours before low on the new moon side of this week's lunar cycle. A hard northeast would do the opposite, dropping the bay a couple of degrees and pushing the bass off the structure. I'd be watching the Ponquogue Bridge pilings on the first quiet, humid night after this next frontal passage; that is historically when the weakfish bite goes from a rumor to a pattern. If 44025 comes back online before the weekend, the first reading worth watching is the inlet-mouth surface temperature against the shelf number — anything north of a five-degree spread and the night outgoing becomes the only tide that matters.

Without live buoy data the report is necessarily structural rather than surgical, but the seasonal architecture of this bay is doing exactly what it should be doing in the second week of June, and the fish are responding accordingly. Fish the outgoing, fish it after dark, and let the inlet do the work.

reports.headline: Block Island bass window opens as June thermal stack sets up over the Ledge
reports.subhead: With 44097 reporting intermittently and 44025 dark, the read is by inference — but the seasonal thermal gradient is on schedule and bait is staged.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this beat is compromised this morning. Buoy 44025 south of Long Island is offline, and 44097 southeast of Block has been intermittent on the water-temperature channel, leaving the published SST package from June 10 as the cleanest snapshot available. That package and the seasonal trajectory through early June put the surface layer around the island in the low-to-mid 60s, with the Southwest Ledge sitting near the leading edge of the thermal front that separates warmer Block Island Sound water inside from the cooler, more oxygenated slug pushing up the shelf edge. Wind has been workable, seas inside Point Judith have laid down through the week, and the outside has not had the kind of sustained southwest blow that piles up surface chop on the Ledge and kills the drift. In short: the engine is built, even if one of the gauges is out.

What that means for this beat is straightforward. June 12 is the front edge of the trophy bass window at Block. The migration class — the genuine cows, fish that wintered off the Chesapeake mouth and the Hudson Canyon edge — is arriving now to settle into the cool, oxygenated rip water they come here for. The Southwest Ledge is the headline structure, and the North Rip is the secondary play depending on wind angle. The fish that show up first are not slot fish. They are overslot and trophy class, and they are going to set up on the down-current side of the Ledge in 60 to 90 feet, working the bait that the tide rivers off the structure. Live eels on a three-way, or three- to five-ounce bucktails tipped with pork or a slim soft plastic, fished right on the edge of the drop — that is the technique that matches the water this week.

On the ground, the porgy and sea bass picture inside Narragansett Bay and around Newport has been steady since the seabass opener, with the better grade of fish holding on the harder structure off Brenton Reef and the lower Bay ledges rather than the soft mud. Fluke reports from the south side of the island have been uneven — a familiar early-summer pattern where the tide is still running too hard on the new and full phases to hold a controlled drift on the deeper edges, and the better fish are coming on the slack-to-building stages closer to the beach in 30 to 45 feet. The drift problem is real and it is geometric, not a bait issue: when the southwest wind opposes the outgoing, the boats spin and the rigs hang. Pick your tide.

The blackfish bite around the wind farm towers and the natural Block boulder fields continues to be a structure story rather than a temperature story, and that fishery is shoulder-season anyway. The signal worth tracking right now is bass. Bait — sand eels on the south side, bunker pods working up from Point Judith, squid still around on the warmer nights — is in position. The water is in the band stripers want. The fish are here or arriving within days.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variables are wind direction and the moon. We are building toward the full moon later in the month, which means tides are going to get bigger before they get smaller, and the Ledge will fish best on the back side of the bigger stages — the last two hours of the ebb into the first of the flood after dark is the classic Southwest Ledge trophy window, and that window gets sharper as the moon fills. If the forecast southwest holds light, the night eel bite should turn on hard by the weekend. A hard onshore blow would push the surface layer warmer and shove the bait tight to the beach, which would shift the program toward the North Rip on the dropping tide. I would be on the Ledge at slack-to-ebb after dark before I would be anywhere else on this beat this week.

The data gaps are real and worth naming — without 44025 and with 44097 unreliable, the precise SST number on the Ledge today is an inference rather than a reading. But the seasonal clock, the bait position, and the structure are all telling the same story. The first serious bass of the Block Island summer are on the board.

reports.headline: Point bite holds on diamond jigs as offshore buoy network goes dark
reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and 44097 thermal data intermittent, the read on Block Island Sound rests on structure, tide, and bait behavior rather than fresh SST.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this stretch of coast is dark this morning. NDBC 44025 — the Long Island buoy that anchors any honest read on what's pushing into the Sound — has its sensor array offline, and 44097 down toward Block Island is feeding intermittent water temperature data. The most recent SST package in the regional catalog is dated June 10, so the satellite read on the rip is roughly 48 hours stale. That's the honest disclosure. What we do have is the seasonal frame: mid-June at the Point typically puts surface water in the upper 50s to very low 60s, with the rip line acting as a convergence between cooler Block Island Sound water sliding south on the ebb and warmer south-side water riding the flood up around the Lighthouse. Without a fresh buoy number I'm not going to pin a decimal on it, but the bait and bass behavior described over the past week is consistent with that classic early-summer thermal seam still being intact rather than blown out.

What that means for the beat is straightforward. The rip is fishing the way the rip is supposed to fish in the second week of June — bass stacked on the structure, willing to eat metal in the column, and sized up rather than schoolie-grade. When the thermal break is set up properly along the Lighthouse rip and out across North Bar, the larger class of fish holds on the down-current side of the boulders, using the structure to ambush sand eels and small herring getting tumbled through. That's a diamond jig bite, not a topwater bite, and the recent intelligence coming off the charter fleet confirms exactly that — multiple overslot fish to the mid-20-pound class, with the bulk of the catch sitting clearly above the slot rather than the 28-to-31 window we saw dominating in May.

North Bar on the ebb has been the higher-percentage piece for the bigger fish. The current ripping across the bar against a southerly breeze stands the water up and concentrates bait against the structure, and the fish are sitting in the 35 to 55 foot range depending on tide stage. Run the jig down, crank it ten turns, drop it back — the hits have been coming on the fall as often as on the lift, which tells you the fish are looking up and the bait is suspended rather than pinned to the bottom. Shagwong on the flood has been the second piece, particularly for boats wanting a softer ride, and Turtle Cove has held fish on the change for the surf and light-tackle crowd working bucktails along the boulder field.

Fluke on the south-side drops are doing what they should be doing for the calendar — a high ratio of shorts with a workable keeper bite on the better drifts, and the bigger fish coming on bucktail-and-Gulp combinations rather than dead-sticked bait. Sea bass are mixed in heavily on the same structure, which is the tell that the bottom temperature is right in the pocket where both species overlap before the fluke push further inshore into the skinny water as June rolls on. Porgies have set up on the harbor structure and the rockier pieces in Fort Pond Bay. Blackfish season is closed and weakfish remain a ghost on this end of the Island, as they have been for years.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variable is wind. A sustained southwest flow will keep the south-side drift comfortable and push warmer surface water against the Point, which tightens the thermal seam and concentrates bass on the rip. A backing northeast — even moderate — will dirty up North Bar, push the rip south, and force the better bite to Shagwong and inside. The moon is working away from full toward last quarter late in the week, which softens the tide ranges and generally favors the dawn and dusk windows over the midday slack. I'd be watching for the first real sand eel push to firm up; once that bait locks in along the rip, the jig bite goes from good to the kind of week people drive five hours for.

The Point is fishing like the Point in June. Big fish are on structure, the metal is working, and the rip is doing its job. Until 44025 comes back online we're reading the water by what it's producing rather than by what the sensors say, which is how this place was fished for a hundred years before any of us had a phone.

reports.headline: Peconic porgy bite finds its rhythm as bay stratifies into early summer pattern
reports.subhead: With the offshore reference buoys dark, the tell is internal: warming inside water on the flood is sorting scup, weakfish, and fluke onto predictable structure.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic picture on the East End this morning is one we are having to read by inference rather than by instrument. The 44025 array south of Moriches remains offline, stripping us of our primary offshore reference, and 44097 off Block Island has been intermittent on water temperature through the past week. The most recent published SST package in the regional catalog is dated June 10, two days stale, and no fresh overnight synthesis has come down the pipe. What we do have is the seasonal trajectory and a consistent run of validated pattern from the prior 72 hours, and both point the same direction: the Peconic estuary is now firmly into its early-summer thermal configuration, with bay water running well ahead of the outside ocean, a sharp gradient at Plum Gut and Orient, and a stratifying water column inside Gardiners and Noyack that is finally behaving like June rather than a stretched-out May.

For this beat that means the bite is consolidating onto the structure and tide stages you would expect for the second week of June, not the laggard pattern we limped through in May. The porgies, which were genuinely difficult earlier in the spring and embarrassed more than a few capable anglers on the Greenlawns and Middle Grounds, have settled in around Shelter Island and the deeper edges off Jessup Neck. The weakfish, conspicuously absent from the traditional April drifts, are now showing as a legitimate bycatch wherever a clam slick is laid down over 18 to 28 feet of sand-and-shell bottom. Fluke are starting to stack in the channel edges between Shelter Island and the South Fork, and the first credible bass reports from the Gut are catching up to the calendar after a slow, cold start.

The porgy story is the headline for the next two weeks. The fish that were scratchy and scattered in early May have grown into a proper June class — quality 16 to 19 inch scup with a real percentage of three-pound jumbos when you get on the right piece of bottom. The pattern that has been producing is a hard-anchored chum approach near the Shelter Island drops and Jessup’s on the flood, with the bite typically taking ten or fifteen minutes to switch on once the slick stretches downtide. Light tides have been better than heavy ones, which fits the moon position and the moderate current we are working with this week. Weakfish keepers to the four-pound class are mixed in, mostly on the tail end of the flood and into the early ebb when the bait pushes off the edges.

Orient and the Gut are the other story worth tracking. Bass were a solid week and a half late entering the bay this spring, with inside-to-outside water-temperature spreads running as wide as ten degrees through mid-May. That gradient has now compressed considerably as the outside water catches up, and the slot-class fish that were stubbornly holding outside the Gut should be moving more freely between Gardiners and the rips off Plum. I would be working the last of the ebb through the turn at Orient with bucktails and soft plastics in the 30 to 40 foot range, particularly on the early-morning low light windows. Bluefish presence remains thin compared to a normal June, and I am not going to manufacture a report that says otherwise — when they show, it will be on the bait, and the bait is still consolidating.

Looking three to five days out, the controlling variables are wind and the continued closing of the inside-outside thermal gap. Any extended southwest sets the Peconic up beautifully — it pushes warm surface water into the heads of Noyack and Northwest Harbor, concentrates bait against the Shelter Island shorelines, and gives you a clean drift through the fluke channels. A hard northeast would scramble that and flatten the porgy chum bite for a tide or two. The moon is building toward the next quarter phase, which will gradually stiffen current and reward anglers who shift to heavier sinkers and tighter anchor sets. If we get a 68-degree surface reading at Orient by the weekend, expect the first real wave of fluke keepers to show on the deeper edges south of Shelter Island.

The Peconic is finally fishing like the Peconic. The porgies are in, the weakfish are a legitimate target again, and the bass are catching up to where they should be. The work for the next two weeks is reading tide stage correctly and keeping a chum slick honest — the fish are telling us what they want, and the water is finally cooperating enough to let us listen.

reports.headline: Sound shore runs on memory as buoy network thins out mid-June
reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and Block Island's thermistor flickering, the North Fork bite has to be read off structure, tide, and the last good SST chart from June 10.
reports.body_markdown:
The instrument picture this morning is thinner than I like. Station 44025 — the Long Island offshore anchor most of us cross-check against — is dark, and 44097 down by Block has been dropping water temperature returns on and off for the better part of a week. The most recent clean SST composite in the pipeline is dated June 10, two days stale, which in mid-June with a warming Sound is enough lag to matter. What that June 10 chart showed, and what the surface still ought to be tracking absent a hard wind event, is a Sound shore creeping into the low-to-mid 60s on the inside, with the deeper push of cooler water still holding through Plum Gut on the flood. Wind has been light out of the southwest, sea state on the Sound side knockdown calm at dawn, building a short chop by midday. No frontal passage in the last 48 hours to flip the column.

What that means for this beat is straightforward even without fresh buoy numbers. The thermal split between the inside Sound water and the colder slug riding through the Gut is the engine right now, and it's firing exactly where it should be — the rockpiles from Horton Point east to Rocky Point, and the approach to Plum Gut itself on the last of the flood into slack. Bass are the headline species, with the class running mixed: a real shot at overslot fish on the deeper structure at Orient, slot and just-under fish working the boulder fields closer to Horton. Porgy have settled onto the hard bottom in numbers a man can count on, and the first honest blackfish chatter is starting where the mussel beds sit on the cooler side of that thermal line. Fluke are around on the sand pockets but they are not the story on the Sound shore — they never really are.

The bait read, as best I can put it together without an overnight wire of reports, is that sand eels are still the dominant forage from Mattituck east, with bunker schools showing in pockets but not blanketing the way they were three weeks back. That favors the slim profile — small soldiers, smaller bucktails with a teaser, and live eels after dark on the Gut approach. The crowd that's been working Orient on the night tides has shifted off chunk and onto live and artificial in the last week, which tells you the fish are keying on movement, not scent, and that matches a Sound that's warmed past the early-season bunker-chunk window.

Oyster cages off the Mattituck-to-Cutchogue stretch are holding bait and holding fish, and that's worth a daylight look on a moving tide if the wind lets you anchor sensibly. Blackfish guys with green crabs are picking at the deeper edges of the cage lines and the natural rock east of there, but the regulation calendar is what it is — read it before you keep one. The porgy bite on clam strips over the gravel from Horton east has been the most reliable daytime play, and a kid with a high-low rig is not going home empty.

Looking out three to five days, the watch items are wind and moon. We're working away from the full and into a weaker tide set, which softens the Gut rip and generally pushes the bigger bass bite shallower and tighter to structure on the Sound shore proper — good news for the rock-hoppers, less good for the Gut drift crowd. If the southwest holds light through the weekend the inside water will keep climbing, and once the shallows push past the mid-60s in earnest the daytime bass bite will compress hard into the first and last hour of light. A wind shift to the northeast, which the longer-range picture hints at but does not promise, would stack bait against the bluffs from Horton to Rocky Point and could turn on a real afternoon blitz window. I'd be watching Horton at first light on the dropping tide, and Orient on the last of the flood after dark, and I would not be in a hurry to believe any single water temperature number until 44025 comes back online and we get a fresh SST package to anchor to.

Fish what's in front of you, read the rips, and don't trust a chart older than the tide you're standing in.

reports.headline: Eastern Sound runs on stale data as 44025 stays dark heading into mid-June
reports.subhead: Primary offshore reference offline and Block Island thermistor flickering — Race and Plum Gut pattern read from structure and seasonal baseline, not live SST.
reports.body_markdown:
The headline reality this morning is that the instruments are quiet. NDBC 44025 — the offshore anchor for any honest Eastern Sound read — is offline, and 44097 down at Block Island is intermittent on water temperature, so the Block thermal signal that normally tells us whether the outside water is loading or stalling is incomplete. The Dr. Fish analyst package did not produce a fresh SST grid for the 12th; the most recent published SST date in the catalog is June 10. Overnight fishing reports did not refresh either. That means today's read is a structural one — bathymetry, tide, moon, and a two-day-old thermal picture — rather than a buoy-driven one. Anyone telling you they have a precise Race surface temp this morning is guessing.

What I can say from the June 10 package and the seasonal baseline is that the Eastern Sound is locked into its early-summer regime. Mid-June here means the inside Peconic and Gardiners water is running materially warmer than what's pumping through the Gut and the Race on each tide — that thermal gradient is the engine. Cold, oxygenated, current-driven water funnels through Plum Gut and The Race; warmer estuary water flushes out on the ebb. Bass stack on the downcurrent side of the boulder fields and the deeper structure where that thermal seam sets up. Without a live SST I'm not putting a number on it, but the seasonal range for this date typically lands the Race in the upper 50s to low 60s on the bottom and the inside bays five to eight degrees warmer at the surface. That spread is what's driving the bite, and there is no reason in the available data to think it has collapsed.

On the ground, the pattern that has been building since the water crossed 52 degrees in mid-May is the one to fish. Plum Gut on the flood has been the more forgiving of the two majors — bucktails on a three-way down 40 to 60 feet, slot and just-over-slot fish working the edges of the rip. The Race holds the bigger class of fish but punishes sloppy drifts; the ebb there with a small pencil popper on a casting rod when the birds start working has put overs on the deck repeatedly through the back half of spring, and there's no oceanographic reason that's changed. Bluefish are in the mix and will tax your terminal — expect to lose bucktails when the gators show, particularly on the Race ebb in full sun.

Fishers Island remains the wild card. The west-side shallow drops in 20 feet are a porgy and sea bass story right now more than a bass story, and the deeper 55-foot drops south and east will be a fall blackfish conversation, not a June one. What the island does offer in June is a structured shoreline where the same thermal seam wraps and bait piles against the rocks on the dropping tide. If the southwest fills in the afternoon — which is the climatological default for this week — the lee side fishes. Weakfish should be a legitimate target in the bays west of the Gut on the warmer end of the tide cycle; mid-June is historically when that bite has its window before the water gets too warm.

Look-ahead is constrained by the data gap, but the mechanics are clear. We are running into the new moon on June 14, which means tides build through the week and current velocity at the Gut and Race peaks. Bigger water moves more bait and stacks more fish on structure, but it also shortens the productive window inside each tide stage — the fish feed hard on the build and the drop, not at peak rip. If 44025 comes back online and shows the offshore water holding in the low 60s, expect the Race ebb to keep producing overs through the weekend. If a hard southwest sets up Saturday into Sunday as the longer-range guidance has been hinting, the Sunday morning ebb at the Gut will be the cleaner play than a beat-up Race.

Until the buoys come back, fish the structure and the moon. The Eastern Sound is doing exactly what mid-June Eastern Sound does, and the absence of fresh numbers doesn't change where the bass are sitting — it just means the rest of us are flying on instruments we already know by feel.

reports.headline: Central Sound report runs on dead reckoning as buoy network thins out
reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and no fresh overnight intel, the mid-June pattern points to a porgy-dominant bottom bite and bass working the shoal rips on moving water.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk is running blind on several key channels this morning. NDBC 44025, the workhorse offshore reference south of the Island, is offline, and 44097 at Block Island is intermittent on water temperature. The Dr. Fish analyst package carries no live SST update for today — the most recent published satellite composite in the catalog is dated June 10, two days stale, and no overnight fishing intelligence cycled through the collection. That means today's read on Central Sound is built from inference: mid-June climatology, the June 10 SST frame, and the structural behavior of this body of water when the offshore reference stations go dark. Expect mid-Sound surface temperatures in the broad mid-60s consistent with the early-June trajectory, with the shallow Connecticut bays running several degrees warmer than the deeper trough north of Stratford Shoal. Wind has been moderate out of the southwest on the local pattern, and without a sea-state update from 44025 I would treat any forecast chop in the central basin as conservative — the fetch from New Haven down to Mattituck builds faster than people remember once the afternoon sea breeze fills in.

What that thermal split means for the beat is straightforward. The inside-outside gradient between the Norwalk Islands flats and the 80-to-100-foot trough off Middle Ground Light is the engine right now. Bass are keyed to the rip lines where that warmer skinny water spills off structure into cooler depth — Stratford Shoal on the back side of the flood, the Middle Ground edges on the early outgoing, and the deeper cuts between the Norwalk Islands when the current is honest. Porgies have settled hard on the 30-to-45-foot rockpiles on both shorelines, and that is the highest-confidence bite in the zone. Fluke are a secondary play on the sand-to-gravel transitions outside Port Jeff and along the CT side from Stamford east, but until we get a cleaner SST read I would not bet the day on doormats — the slot-class bass bite is the better use of fuel.

The pattern on the water over the past several weeks has been a slow, orderly progression rather than a blow-up. The mid-Sound bottom fishery has been carrying more porgies than sea bass keepers, with a heavy ratio of shorts to boxers on the black sea bass — that is normal for the central basin in June, where the keeper-class fish are still staged in deeper, cooler pockets and have not fully moved up onto the shallower structure that the Connecticut side will produce later in the month. Bass reports out of Port Jeff and the CT shoreline have been steady on bunker schools where they can be found, and the night bite in the harbor mouths has been a more reliable pattern than midday open-water work.

Bait is the variable I would track hardest with the buoy network compromised. Spearing have been thick along the harbor edges through late spring, and the first real push of peanut bunker into the inside waters typically lines up with this week-of-June window when shallow water crosses the upper 60s. If you are seeing fresh bunker schools in Smithtown Bay or off the Norwalk Islands, that is your tell that the larger bass are committed to the inside water. Without it, the better fish stay out on Stratford Shoal and the Middle Ground edges and you have to go to them.

The next three to five days are about whether the Atlantic high builds in and gives us a stretch of light southwest wind, which would let the shallow Connecticut water continue to warm and pull bait northward across the basin. If that materializes, the Norwalk Islands bite sharpens on the outgoing and the bottom fleet sees the sea bass keeper ratio improve as those fish slide shallower. A frontal passage with a north or northeast shift would do the opposite — cool the inside water, push bait back out, and concentrate the bass on the deeper structure. I would also be watching for the 44025 array to come back online; until it does, anyone running east of Middle Ground should be conservative on sea-state assumptions and check Execution Rocks and New Haven harbor stations for the best available proxy data.

The water is doing what mid-June water does in this basin — stratifying, warming on the edges, concentrating bait on the structure that holds current. The fish are where the physics says they should be. Run the rips on moving water, anchor the rockpiles on the slack, and do not let the thin data picture this morning talk you out of fishing the spots you already know.

reports.headline: Western Sound bass settle into mid-June bunker pattern as offshore data thins out
reports.subhead: With NDBC 44025 offline and Block Island thermistor intermittent, inside-Sound structure and bait position carry the read this week.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this beat is dark. NDBC 44025 — the Long Island station that anchors our outside-water picture — is offline, and 44097 up at Block Island is feeding intermittent temperature data, so the regional thermal gradient between the Sound and the open shelf has to be inferred rather than measured today. The last clean SST package in the catalog is dated June 10, and nothing has refreshed since. What we do have is two solid weeks of run-up imagery showing the western basin sitting in its classic mid-June posture: an inside body of water roughly four to six degrees warmer than the Race and the eastern Sound, with the thermal step parked somewhere between Eatons Neck and Stratford Shoal. Surface conditions on the western basin have been benign in the short term — light southerlies, a sloppy chop on the afternoon sea breeze, nothing in the way of frontal disruption to scatter bait.

That thermal arrangement is exactly what you want for this part of June on this beat. The inside water is past the 60-degree threshold that wakes up bunker schools and pushes adult bass off their post-spawn lethargy into a hard feed. The colder eastern Sound is still funneling fish westward toward warmer foraging grounds, which is why Execution Rocks, the Matinecock bunker grounds, and the Stepping Stones-to-Hart Island corridor have been the productive triangle. Slot-class fish dominate the population right now, with a respectable percentage of overslot mixed in — a clean reflection of the migratory class that staged here through May not yet having dropped out for the deeper, cooler holes they'll occupy by the Fourth of July.

The bunker have firmed up off Matinecock Point and along the deeper edge running west toward Execution. Boat pressure on the open-water schools has been heavy enough on weekends to put fish down by mid-tide, which is the recurring story on this beat — the bite is real, but it is a moving-water bite that turns off when current slacks and the fleet pinwheels on top of the pods. The reliable hits have been on the harder phases of the outgoing, with live-lined bunker producing the biggest fish and trolled mojos and bunker spoons covering water when the pods get scattered. Topwater work at first light over the Stepping Stones flats has been worth the early alarm clock, particularly on the back end of the outgoing into the bottom of the tide.

Fluke remains a grind across the western basin. The Oyster Bay-to-Lloyd's drift is producing volume but the keeper ratio is poor, and the deeper channel edges off Matinecock and the drop into the main Sound are giving up better-sized fish than the shallow flats. Drift speed has been the issue more than bait — the light wind days are killing the presentation. Porgy fishing has filled in nicely over the structure on the Larchmont and New Rochelle side, and around Hart Island, with the bigger humpbacks showing on the deeper rockpiles. Blackfish season is closed; weakfish remain a wildcard the way they always do here, occasional and welcome rather than a target.

Looking ahead three to five days, the key variable is wind. A sustained southwest breeze of ten to fifteen would set up a textbook afternoon bite by stacking bunker against the north shore of Long Island from Matinecock east, and would put a useful drift on the fluke grounds for the first time in a week. Without a wind shift, expect more of the same — early and late windows on the bass, dead middle of the day, and a fluke bite that rewards the angler willing to run east to find current. The new moon arrives next week and the tides will build through the weekend, which historically tightens the bass bite on Execution and the bridge structure as current velocity increases. Water temperature inside the basin should continue to climb; once the shallow bays push past the upper sixties, the larger adult bunker bodies will start sliding deeper, and the bite geometry shifts off the surface and onto the wire.

This is a get-on-the-water week. The fish are here, the bait is here, and the inside water is doing exactly what mid-June inside water is supposed to do. Pick your tide, pick your structure, and do not waste daylight standing on top of a school that has already gone down. Move, find the next pod, and fish the moving water hard.

reports.headline: Mid-June bait push holds fish from Sandy Hook to Cape May despite thin buoy data
reports.subhead: With offshore reference buoys offline and SST package three days stale, the Jersey beat runs on bunker biology and tide windows this week.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic picture this morning is thinner than I'd like. The 44025 sensor array — the workhorse offshore reference for the New York Bight and the buoy I lean on hardest to read what's coming down the Jersey coast — is offline, and 44097's water temperature feed up at Block Island is intermittent. The most recent SST composite in the pipeline is dated June 10, two and a half days behind real time. That's a gap worth naming up front, because anyone telling you exactly what the thermocline is doing off Barnegat Ridge this morning is guessing. What we can say with confidence is seasonal: by the second week of June, inside waters from Raritan Bay down through Great Bay are in the upper 60s to low 70s, the ocean wash from Sandy Hook to Island Beach is running cooler in the low-to-mid 60s, and Cape May rips are sitting at the warm end of that range as the southern bight pulls in shelf water. Bunker are the dominant bait coast-wide right now, with sand eels still present in the cleaner ocean sand south of Barnegat Inlet.

That thermal split — warm estuary, cooler suds — is what shapes the next week of fishing on this beat. The big resident bass that pushed into Raritan Bay in April and gorged through May are now a mixed body of fish: some have slid out around Sandy Hook and are working the ocean side from the Rip down to the Shrewsbury Rocks, others are still hammering bunker pods inside the bay on the western shoals. Down south, the bait-and-switch is fluke season in earnest, with the ocean structure off Manasquan, Axel Carlson, and the Barnegat Ridge holding keeper-class fish on the drift, and weakfish reappearing in the Mullica and back-bay channels of Great Bay on the cooler dawn tides.

Raritan Bay is still the headline. The bunker schools are thick enough that the pattern hasn't changed much in two weeks — find the bait, find the fish, and the bigger class of bass is keying on adult menhaden in the channel edges off the Reach and around Romer Shoal. Live-lining a snagged bunker on a 9/0 circle remains the high-percentage play for an overslot, with the outgoing into the slack producing the cleaner shots. Plug guys throwing big swimmers at first light off the Hook tip and along the false hook beach have been getting their licks in on the slot fish. The Shark River and Manasquan Inlet scenes have shifted toward fluke, with the better keepers coming on the outgoing through the inlet mouths on bucktail-and-gulp combos in the 1.5 to 3 ounce range depending on current. Down at Cape May, the rips are firing on the change of tide, with weakfish showing in Delaware Bay on the channel edges after dark.

Blackfish are closed in New Jersey waters until August, so set that aside. Porgy fishing on the inshore reefs and rockpiles off Sandy Hook and along the Shrewsbury Rocks has come on strong, and the bigger humpback fish are mixed in with the sea bass on the Axel Carlson and Garden State South pieces. Clams will out-produce squid for the better class of porgy.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variable is wind. Any sustained southerly stacks warm surface water against the beach and pushes the cooler ocean water further offshore, which tightens the bass to the inlet mouths and the bayside structure and hurts the ocean suds bite. A clocking northeast — even modest — drops the wash temperature, knocks the bunker schools tight to the beach, and lights up the Island Beach and Long Beach Island suds for a day or two before it gets sloppy. The moon is building toward full late in the week, which means stronger tides through Raritan, Manasquan, and Barnegat, and I'd be on the outgoing two hours either side of bottom of the tide at the inlet mouths. If the 44025 array comes back online before the weekend, watch for any sign of cooler water pushing south along the coast — that's the trigger that resets the suds bite from Sandy Hook to Barnegat.

The fish are here, the bait is here, and the calendar is doing the heavy lifting. Read the wind, fish the tide edges hard, and don't overthink it — June on the Jersey Shore rewards anglers who put their plug in the bunker pod and let the bass do the rest.

reports.headline: Peconic porgy bite finds its rhythm as estuary stratifies into mid-June pattern
reports.subhead: Primary offshore reference at 44025 is dark and Block Island temps are intermittent, so the read leans on the estuary's own thermal signature and last week's SST package.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic estuary sits in its classic mid-June posture this morning, even if the offshore instruments aren't doing us any favors. NDBC 44025 south of Moriches is offline, knocking out the primary Long Island shelf reference, and the Block Island station at 44097 has been intermittent on water temperature. That leaves the most recent regional SST package, dated June 10, as the best available read on surface structure, and it shows the Peconics running well ahead of the open Sound and the ocean side — the expected springtime gradient, with the shallow bay basins acting as a solar collector while Plum Gut and the Race continue to flush cooler, denser water in on every flood. Wind has been manageable, sea state inside Gardiners is light, and the bay surface is behaving like a stratified pond between tide changes.

What that means for this beat is straightforward. The estuary is warm enough now that scup are locked onto their summer structure, fluke are settling into the deeper sand channels around Shelter Island and the mouth of Noyack, and weakfish — which have been a question mark all spring — are finally showing in numbers worth targeting on a dedicated drift. The bass piece has largely shifted out of the inside bay and concentrated at Plum Gut and Orient Point, where the colder Sound water moving through the Gut keeps bait pinned and gives the fish a reason to stay. Inside the bay, the slot-class striper bite is a dawn-and-dusk game on the shallow flats off Jessup's Neck and the Cedar Point side; midday belongs to the bottom fleet.

The porgy story has straightened out considerably from the rough early-May stretch. The Middle Grounds and the Greenlawns are producing again, but the fish have been particular about tide and chum — a slack arrival, ten minutes for the slick to set up, and the bite turning on as the current builds. Jessup's on the flood has been the most consistent producer for jumbos in the 16-to-18-inch class, with some 19-inch fish in the mix and the occasional three-pounder for crews willing to cull. The pattern this spring has rewarded patience and precise anchoring far more than mileage; running and gunning has burned more fuel than fish. Weakfish are mixed into the porgy drifts in the deeper edges, and a handful of keepers to four pounds have come on the same clam baits intended for scup.

Fluke have begun to organize on the channel edges between Shelter Island and the North Fork, with the better fish coming from 18 to 30 feet on a moving tide. Bucktail-and-Gulp remains the workhorse, but as water temps continue to climb the bigger fish are responding to a slower presentation with a teaser above. Bluefish have been spotty inside the bay — a pattern that's been holding for more than a season now — but Gardiners and the rips off Orient have produced cocktail blues and the occasional alligator on topwater at first light. Blackfish are essentially done for the recreational fleet until fall; the focus on hard structure now belongs to the porgy and sea bass crowd.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variable is whether the estuary stratification holds or gets mixed by a wind event. Without 44025 in the picture I can't track an offshore swell signal cleanly, so I'd be watching the marine forecast for any sustained southwesterly above 15 knots, which would push warmer surface water into the upper bay and likely accelerate the weakfish bite in Noyack and the Robins Island lee. A continuation of the current light pattern keeps the porgy bite locked where it is and lets the fluke fishery mature on schedule. The Gut bass will fade as the Sound warms past the upper 50s, and once that happens the inside bay flats become the primary striper game for the rest of the month.

The estuary is doing exactly what it should be doing in the second week of June. The fish are where the temperature gradient and the tide tell them to be, the chum-and-anchor program is paying for crews who run it properly, and the absence of clean offshore data is a reason to read the water carefully, not a reason to stay at the dock.

reports.headline: Montauk runs on instinct as offshore buoys go dark mid-June
reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and 44097's thermistor blinking in and out, the Point's early-summer bass pattern has to be read off the rocks and the bait.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for the East End is dark this morning. NDBC 44025 — the Long Island station every Montauk skipper checks before he turns the key — has its sensor array offline, and 44097 down on the Block Island approach is feeding intermittent water-temperature data, so the thermal picture out past the Pollock Rip has to be assembled by hand. There is no fresh SST imagery beyond the June 10 package in the catalog, which means surface structure two days old at best. What we do know from that last clean look: the inshore South Side was already running noticeably warmer than the rip line off the Lighthouse, and the Block Island Sound side, behind Shagwong, was the cooler pocket. With light wind through the overnight and no major frontal mixing, that gradient should still be roughly intact.

For the Point, mid-June with a stable two-body thermal setup is textbook. The bass are off their pre-spawn slog and into a feeding posture, and the warmer South Side band from Turtle Cove west toward the Radar Tower is where the bait — sand eels first, with bunker pushing in behind them — concentrates on the morning ebb. The cooler Sound-side water behind North Bar and Shagwong is holding the bigger class of fish that don't want to sit in 60-plus surface temps during the day. That is the split I would fish to right now: slot and just-over fish on the South Side at first light on plugs and bucktails, and the heavier overslot class on the Sound side during the strong tide windows, worked deep with wire and tube, or jigged off the boulders.

Diamond-jig work along the Point itself has been producing the kind of mixed bag that tells you the fish are stacked but picky — a lot of clear overs, a handful of slot fish, very few shorts. That is a sand-eel signature. When the bait is thin and uniform, the bigger fish out-compete the schoolies on the rip and you get a top-heavy box. The classic North Bar drift on the dropping tide into the rip has been the higher-percentage move than running and gunning the boulder fields, and the fish are holding tight to the structure rather than scattered in open water. Shagwong Reef on the flood, with the current pushing bait up onto the shallow shelf, is the other tide-stage play and it has been giving up a quieter but more consistent bite for the live-eel crowd at last light.

The fluke story on the South Side drop is just beginning to round into form. Drifts from the Lighthouse southwest toward Frisbees have been turning over a lot of fish with the keeper ratio still mediocre — expect to grind through shorts to find the 19- to 22-inch class — but a real five-pound fish is in the mix on every trip now, and the sea bass bycatch is heavy enough that you want a teaser rigged at all times. Porgies are stacked on the harder bottom inside Fort Pond Bay and along the Sound-side rockpiles, with blackfish season closed but the fish very much present and snapping at clam baits meant for scup. Bluefish remain spotty at the Point itself, more of a chopper-class fish blowing through on the tide than a resident body, but Turtle Cove has had legitimate pre-dawn topwater windows for anyone willing to be there before the sun.

Looking ahead three to five days, the variable to watch is wind. A protracted southwest breeze, which is the climatological norm for mid-June here, will pile warmer surface water up against the South Side and steepen the thermocline, which would push the larger bass even more firmly onto the Sound side and concentrate the South Side bite into the first and last light windows. If we get an east wind event, that flips — cold upwelling comes up the South Side, the bait scatters, and the Sound side warms enough to soften that bite too. Without 44025 online, the first read on any shift will be from 44017 to the east and from boat-deck thermometers. Moon is building toward full late next week, which will hand us bigger tides and a stronger nighttime eel bite along the boulder line from Jones Reef to the Lighthouse.

The Point is fishing the way the Point is supposed to fish in early June — quality over quantity, structure over open water, tide stage over hero spots. Run the ebb on the South Side at first light, work the Sound side hard on the flood, and respect the fact that the biggest fish in the zone right now are not where the boats are stacked up.

reports.headline: Inlet thermal gradient sets up the June night bite as offshore reference data thins out
reports.subhead: With NDBC 44025 offline and 44097 reporting intermittently, the bay-to-ocean temperature differential at Shinnecock Inlet becomes the controlling variable.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this stretch of the South Shore is dark today. NDBC 44025 — the Long Island buoy that normally anchors any honest read on shelf water temperature and sea state — has its sensor array offline, and 44097 off Block Island is feeding water temperature only intermittently. The most recent SST package in the pipeline carries a June 10 date, two days stale, and no overnight angler reports came in to ground-truth it. That puts the burden on the inlet itself as the instrument. What I can say from the water and from the last clean satellite pass is that the bay-to-ocean differential is now firmly in its June configuration: the back of Shinnecock Bay, from the Ponquogue flats east toward Tiana, is running warm and shallow under long daylight, while the ocean side of the inlet is still pulling in cooler, denser water on the flood. That gradient is the engine right now.

For my beat, that means the inlet is doing exactly what it does in the second week of June. Bass that staged through May are now keyed to the thermal break that sets up on the dropping tide, when warm bay water funnels out past the jetty tips and meets the cooler ocean water along the rip line. The slot-class fish are holding on the ocean side of that seam, ambushing bait that gets swept out of the bay. Overslot fish — the ones worth fishing for and releasing carefully — are working the deeper scour holes on the east jetty side in 18 to 25 feet, particularly on the back half of the outgoing into the bottom of the tide. This is a soft-plastic and swimming-plug window, not a chunk window. The water is too lively and the bait too mobile for sitting on bait.

Inside the bay, the Ponquogue Bridge is in its early-summer rhythm. Weakfish typically thread the bridge pilings on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of slack, working the shadow line under the lights. With bay water now well into the upper-fifties to low-sixties range based on what the area normally runs in mid-June and what limited satellite signal we have, that fishery should be live for anyone willing to fish small — pink and pearl plastics on quarter-ounce heads, fished slow against the current seam. Fluke have moved off the deep channel and are spreading onto the drifts between the inlet and the Ponquogue channel, with the better fish on the sand-to-mud transitions in 12 to 18 feet. Bucktail and Gulp is the rig; long drifts on the moving tide beat short drifts on slack every time this month.

The Shinnecock Canal continues to function as the conveyor between systems. Bait pushed by the Peconic tides funnels through on the south-running cycle and stacks at the bay mouth of the canal, which is why the western end of the bay near the canal has been holding fish disproportionate to its size. Blackfish season is closed but porgies are thick on the rockier bottom along the north shore of the bay and around the bridge abutments — a daytime fallback when the wind kills the inlet drift. Bluefish presence has been spotty rather than blitz-grade, which fits a year where the bunker schools haven't fully consolidated inside the bay yet.

Looking three to five days out, the question is whether 44025 comes back online and gives us a clean offshore number, because without it we are reasoning from inference. The moon is building toward full later this month, which will stiffen the tides and lengthen the productive outgoing window at the inlet — that is the next mechanical change worth planning around. If a south or southwest wind sets up for two consecutive afternoons, expect the warm bay water to pile against the inlet and intensify the thermal seam on the drop; that is the night I'd be out on the east jetty side with a dark bottle plug. A hard northeast shift would scramble it and push the bait deeper into the bay, in which case the Ponquogue Bridge becomes the play.

The inlet is fishing the way June inlets fish when the gradient is right, and the gradient is right. The data picture is thinner than I'd like, but the water is telling a clear enough story for anyone willing to fish the outgoing in the dark.

reports.headline: Moriches Inlet runs on inference as offshore buoys go dark mid-June
reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and 44097 intermittent, the bay's internal thermal gradient becomes the primary read for inlet bass and skinny-water fluke.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this zone is dark today. NDBC 44025 — the Long Island buoy that normally anchors any honest read on shelf water temperature and sea state south of Moriches — is offline, and 44097 at Block Island is reporting intermittent water-temperature data. The most recent SST composite in the pipeline is dated June 10, two days stale, and no fresh overnight intelligence has come through the wire. That means today's report is built on inference: the trajectory of the past ten days of SST imagery, the seasonal calendar, and what the inlet itself is telling anyone willing to read it. Mid-June on this beat historically puts inside bay water in the upper 60s on the flood and pushing low 70s on a hard ebb under sun, with ocean water outside Moriches Inlet running five to eight degrees cooler. That delta is the engine.

For the Moriches system specifically, an unresolved offshore number does not change the mechanism — it just raises the cost of being wrong about it. The thermal gradient across the inlet throat is what concentrates bass on the ebb and pulls cooler, cleaner water across the flats on the flood. With the bay warming faster than the ocean in June, the last two hours of outgoing through the inlet is where I'd be putting time in: bass stacking on the ocean-side rips off the east jetty, working the scour holes in 18 to 24 feet where the channel dumps into the Atlantic. Slot-class fish are the realistic target — the overslot push that ran through here in late May has largely moved east toward Shinnecock and Montauk, and what remains is resident-grade fish keyed on bunker fragments and spearing rather than the big herring profile.

Inside the bay, the fluke story is the one that matters most this week. The skinny-water program out of the Forge River and along the Tuthill Point flats has been the dominant pattern, with the better fish — five pounds and up — coming on light jigs in three to eight feet during the cooler ends of the tide cycle. The pattern that emerged last summer has reasserted itself: when bay water shoves past 78 degrees in the afternoon, the bite shuts off hard and the fish either bury or slide to the deeper channel edges where the inlet's cooler exchange water reaches. That makes morning outgoing into the first of the flood the productive window, and it makes the edges of the East and West Channels — particularly the drop from four feet to eleven feet on the south side of the bay — the right structure when the flats go warm.

Cupsogue remains the surf story, and it is a tide story before it is a bait story. The wash on the ocean side at Cupsogue has been fishing best on the last of the outgoing into slack, when the inlet plume carries bait out and stripers set up just outside the break. Bluefish are mixed in and have been the more reliable pull on metal during daylight; the bass bite is largely a dawn and dusk affair on bucktails and soft plastics. Weakfish reports inside the bay have been thin but not absent — the Tuthill Point and Seatuck shorelines on a night incoming tide are the classic move, and the water temperature is right for it.

Looking three to five days out, the controlling variable is wind. A sustained southwest breeze stacks warm surface water against the north shore of the bay and drives bay temperatures higher faster, which compresses the fluke window and pushes the better fish to channel edges sooner each day. If we get a clean northeast rotation, it flushes the bay, drops surface temps two or three degrees overnight, and resets the flats bite for a day or two. The moon is building toward the full on the 19th, which means tides will be gaining amplitude through the weekend — stronger ebbs through Moriches Inlet, more aggressive scour on the bayside shoals, and a sharper thermal exchange at the throat. That favors the inlet bass program over the flats program as the week progresses.

The honest framing for today is that the ocean side is being read by proxy until 44025 comes back online. The inlet itself, the bay temperature trajectory, and the moon are doing enough of the work to fish with confidence — provided anglers respect that the afternoon shutoff is real and that the productive water in June moves with the tide, not with the clock.

reports.headline: Bay warms ahead of ocean as Fire Island fleet works a split-temperature front
reports.subhead: With offshore buoy 44025 dark and the SST package five days stale, the controlling variable is the inside-outside thermal gradient stacking bait at the inlet.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this beat is gone today — NDBC 44025 south of Fire Island is offline, and the Block Island station 44097 is feeding intermittent water-temperature data. The most recent published SST composite in the pipeline is dated June 10, two days old going on three, which means the satellite read on the inside-outside break is a stale picture rather than a live one. Working from what is available and from the seasonal trajectory, mid-June on the South Shore typically puts Great South Bay surface temps in the mid-to-upper 60s while the ocean side of Fire Island lags several degrees cooler, and nothing in the available data suggests this year is off that script. Wind has been light enough through the week to let the bay stratify and the inlet to run clean on the ebb.

What that split does to my zone is predictable and it is already showing up on the rails. A warmer bay pushing out through Fire Island Inlet on the drop meets colder, denser ocean water and stacks bait right at the rip — sand eels and spearing on the ocean side, bunker fry and grass shrimp pulsing out of the bay. That is a fluke conveyor belt on the outgoing along the Robert Moses bridge channels and the inlet flats in 18 to 35 feet, and it is a striped bass setup at the inlet mouth and along the Democrat Point rip on the back end of the ebb into the first of the flood. Sea bass and porgies are holding on the near-ocean structure outside the inlet now that bottom temps have climbed into their comfort band, and the wreck and rockpile bite a few miles off the beach has been the most consistent body of water out there.

The Captree open-boat fleet has been bending rods hard on mixed-bag bottom trips just outside the inlet — sea bass limits coming quickly on jigs and teasers, porgies layered in with them, ling showing on clam, and even a stray cod and chub mackerel in the mix. That is a classic early-summer signature for water in the 58–62°F range over the near-shore lumps, and it tells me the thermocline has not yet set up hard enough to push the sea bass deeper. Inside the bay, the striped bass bite has continued to favor soft plastics over bait on the night tides out of Captree, with a healthy mix of slot and overslot fish working the channel edges. The clam-and-doggie problem that plagued the May night trips has eased as water warmed and the spiny dogfish thinned out of the inlet, but plastics — paddletails and Bass Assassins on a half-ounce to one-ounce head — are still outfishing chunk on most drifts.

Fluke reports out of the inlet have been steady rather than spectacular, with the usual heavy ratio of shorts to keepers along the bridge abutments and the channel edges off Sore Thumb. The better class of fish has been coming from the ocean side of the inlet on longer drifts in 30 to 50 feet, working bucktails tipped with Gulp on the down-tide rod. Weakfish remain a wildcard — the bay has the salinity and the bait to hold them, and a few are around, but it is not yet the kind of bite that justifies targeting them over a fluke drift.

Looking out three to five days, the move I am watching is wind direction and the position of that thermal front. A southwest breeze building through the weekend will push warmer surface water against the Fire Island beach and could finally tip the ocean-side suds into the mid-60s, which is the threshold where the bunker schools that have been milling outside start filtering into the inlet in numbers. If that happens, the inlet bite shifts from a finesse plastics game to a live-lined or snagged-bunker game on the outgoing, and the overslot class of bass moves up in the column. The new moon on June 15 will also juice the tidal range, meaning stronger currents and a sharper, more compressed feeding window on each tide change.

For now, I would be working the Robert Moses bridges first light on the last of the outgoing with plastics, running outside to the rockpiles mid-morning for a mixed-bag bottom session, and watching the ocean-side surf at Democrat Point any evening the wind lays down. The split between bay and ocean is what is driving everything in this zone right now, and until the offshore buoy comes back online we are reading the water with our eyes and our drifts.

reports.headline: Data-thin Thursday at Jones Inlet as primary buoys go dark mid-June
