reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and 44097 reporting intermittently, the bite read leans on seasonal pattern and shoreline signal rather than live SST.
reports.body_markdown:
The analyst desk is running on fumes this morning. The 44025 sensor array — the workhorse reference twenty-odd miles south of Fire Island that normally anchors any honest Jones Inlet report — is offline, and 44097 out toward Block Island has been coughing up intermittent water-temperature returns. The most recent satellite SST package in the catalog is dated June 10, two days stale, and no fresh overnight intelligence was logged. That means no clean number to hang on the inside-versus-outside thermal gradient today, and any specific Fahrenheit figure you see floating around the docks this morning is somebody's guess, not measurement. What we do know is seasonal: by the second week of June the back of Hempstead Bay is typically running well into the mid-60s on the flood and pushing toward 70 on a sun-baked afternoon ebb, while the ocean side of Jones Inlet itself lags by several degrees as cleaner Atlantic water punches in on every incoming tide. That gradient is the engine, and it is almost certainly running right now whether or not the buoy is reporting it.

For this beat, a stalled data feed in mid-June doesn't change the playbook much — it just forces you to fish the structure you trust. The thermal break sits right inside the inlet throat, where warmer bay water meeting cooler ocean wash sets up a feeding line that bass and bluefish lean on hard during the back half of the outgoing. Fluke should be holding on the cleaner, cooler sand south and east of the inlet, with the Sloop Channel edge and the drifts south of the Meadowbrook holding the better class of fish on the incoming. Weakfish — and there are more of them in this bay than there have been in fifteen years — are a slack-tide and low-light story, sitting deep in the bay on the channel edges off Freeport and the Wantagh marshes.

The surf side has shifted into its early-summer rhythm. The big bunker pods that lit up Jones Beach in May have largely moved through, and what's left on the beach is a mixed bag — resident bass working sand eels and spearing at first light along the Field 6 cuts and the bar east of the inlet, with the better grade of fish caught on dropping water before sunrise. The bluefish presence inside the bay has firmed up over the past two weeks; the snapper class is showing as expected for the calendar, and the harbor blues in the 18-to-22-inch range are running the bait edges on the incoming around the bridges. On the fluke side, the drifts south of Jones Inlet have been holding fish but the ratio of shorts to keepers is what it always is in June — you'll work through a lot of 16- and 17-inch fish before you find a true doormat, and the better-class fish are coming off the cleaner ocean drifts in 30 to 50 feet rather than the bay drifts inside.

Bait pattern matches the water. Bucktails dressed with squid strips or Gulp continue to outproduce strictly natural baits on the fluke drift when the wind cooperates, and the soft-plastic shad-on-jighead presentation that took over the late-fall bass game last year is carrying right into the early summer pattern for bay bass holding around the Meadowbrook and Loop pilings. Live snappers, once they bulk up another inch, will be the move for bay blues and any bonus bass by late June.

Looking out three to five days, the controlling variable is wind. With no live offshore wave data to lean on, I'd watch the marine forecast more carefully than usual — a sustained southwest blow over 15 knots will stack warm surface water against the South Shore beaches and accelerate the bay warm-up, which pushes the fluke bite out of the back and concentrates it on the ocean drifts off Short Beach and east toward Gilgo. A clean northeast piece of weather, conversely, will flush cooler water into the inlet and trigger the better tide-line bite right in the throat on the outgoing. The new moon on the 14th sharpens current speed mid-week, which favors the bridge bite on the incoming and the inlet tide-line on the outgoing.

Fish the structure, fish the tide, and don't trust any temperature number you can't tie to a working sensor. The pattern is mid-June — the data just hasn't caught up to the calendar this morning.

reports.headline: Jamaica Bay sits in the June thermal pivot with offshore reference data dark
reports.subhead: With Buoy 44025 offline and no fresh SST package since June 10, the bay's own thermal engine is the read — and it's pushing fluke and bass into predictable lanes.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this stretch of coast is dark. NDBC 44025 — the Long Island buoy that normally anchors any honest discussion of what the nearshore Atlantic is doing — is offline, and 44097 up at Block Island has been intermittent on water temperature. The most recent published SST package in the catalog is two days stale, dated June 10. That is the honest dateline of this report: we are reading the bay by its own signals right now, not by a clean offshore handshake. What we do know is structural and seasonal. Mid-June in Jamaica Bay means the back-bay flats have run well into the upper 60s on afternoon floods while Rockaway Inlet and the ocean side of Breezy still sit several degrees cooler on the outgoing. That delta — warm bay water dumping through the inlet against cooler ocean water — is the engine that runs this beat in June, and nothing in the available data suggests it is not running on schedule.

What that thermal structure means on the ground is straightforward. The Marine Parkway Bridge is the choke point where that warm bay water accelerates on the drop, and bass stage on the down-current side of the pilings waiting for whatever the tide delivers. This is a slot-class fishery right now — schoolie to low-slot fish in the 24 to 30 inch range are the bread and butter, with the occasional overslot mixed in around the bigger moons. Fluke have been in the bay long enough to have settled into their summer lies along the channel edges off Ruffle Bar and the drop into Beach Channel. And the inlet itself, particularly the rockpile at Breezy, is fishing the way Breezy fishes in June: live bait when you can get it, bucktails when you cannot.

The pattern that has been firming up over the last week is a clean two-tide day for anyone willing to work it. First light on the last of the outgoing through the Marine Parkway has been producing slot bass on bucktails and soft plastics worked tight to the bridge shadow line — the fish are using the shadow seam as an ambush point and a four to six inch paddletail on a half-ounce to one-ounce head is the right tool. As the tide flips and the bay starts to fill, the fluke program kicks in along the Rockaway Inlet channel edges in 18 to 25 feet, with the bucktail-and-teaser rig doing what it always does when water clarity is reasonable. The back-bay flats — the broken bottom east of Canarsie Pier and the marsh edges around the Cross Bay Bridge — are holding short fluke and the first scattered weakfish of the season, with a few keeper weaks mixed into the shorts on the incoming.

Bunker are in the bay in workable numbers and that is the variable that matters most over the next week. Where the bunker concentrate — typically the deeper holes off the airport and the channel south of the Cross Bay — is where the overslot bass will set up at dawn and dusk. Snag-and-drop is the move when you find a tight pod. The porgy and blackfish picture is secondary in June but the structure around the Marine Parkway abutments and the inlet jetty rocks will give up porgies on clams and small jigs for anyone who wants a cooler full of fish without chasing.

Looking three to five days out, the controlling variables are wind and moon. We are working toward the next moon phase, which will sharpen the tides through the inlet and the bridge — that historically lights up the Marine Parkway bite on the back side of the drop. A sustained southwest wind would push warmer ocean water against the south side of Breezy and compress the inlet thermal break, which tightens the bass to the rockpile. A hard easterly would do the opposite, stack cool water on the beach and push the program back inside the bay. Without a working 44025, I am watching the inlet itself for the read — water clarity, bait behavior, and where the terns are working at the change of tide.

The bay is doing in June what the bay does in June. The offshore data is thin this week and that is worth saying out loud, but the structural fishery — bridge bass on the outgoing, fluke on the channel edges, weakfish starting to show on the flats — is on the clock and on the calendar. Fish the tide, fish the shadow lines, and pay attention to where the bunker move next.

reports.headline: Race and Plum Gut bass dialed in on bucktail drifts as offshore reference data thins
reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and 44097 intermittent, the eastern Sound bite is being read off tide stage and structure rather than fresh SST telemetry.
reports.body_markdown:
The primary offshore reference for this beat is dark today. NDBC 44025 south of Long Island is offline, and 44097 down by Block Island is intermittent on water temperature, leaving no clean SST handoff into the eastern Sound this morning. The most recent published SST package in the catalog is dated June 10, two days stale, and no fresh overnight oceanographic synthesis came across the wire. That means we are reading the water off tide tables, structure, and the trajectory of the last week's pattern rather than a buoy print I'd normally lead with. What we do know: we are squarely into the mid-June window when the Race, Plum Gut and the Orient rip are running their early-summer program — surface water through the eastern Sound should be sitting in the low-to-mid 60s based on the seasonal trajectory off recent 44097 partials, with deeper Race water several degrees colder where the 5-knot ebb scours bottom over the 200-foot holes.

That thermal split is the engine right now. Cold, oxygenated water ripping over structure on the big tides is exactly what stacks slot-class bass in the eddies behind Valiant Rock and the Sluiceway, and it's why the bucktail-and-shad bite over deep water has been the controlling technique rather than topwater. Plum Gut is fishing more honestly than the Race on the ebb — fewer boats, cleaner drifts, and a tighter window — while the Race is paying out better numbers but demanding heavy iron to keep contact on the 100-plus-foot drops. Overslot fish are mixed into the Race drifts; the Gut has been more of a true slot game with the occasional 37-incher on the swing.

The pattern over the past two weeks has been consistent: ebb tide producing better than flood at the Gut for boat traffic reasons alone, with the bass holding tight to the rip line and crushing 3-ounce bucktails tipped or worked clean off three-way rigs. When the rip stands up hardest near max ebb, the surface program comes alive — small pencils into the foam are putting fish on the deck without needing to grind bottom. Bluefish are in the mix at the Race and they are the toll booth: expect to donate tackle once the gorillas key in, and treat the bluefish arrival as the signal to reposition rather than re-rig. Fluke are filling in on the sand edges off Orient and the Gardiners side, and porgies are thick enough on mid-Sound humps to be a legitimate backup plan when the rips go quiet on the slack.

Fishers Island is the quiet story. The west-side shallows and the rockpiles that fish so hard in the fall for blackfish are holding bass right now on the low-light edges, and the boat traffic out there is a fraction of what's stacked up at the Gut on a weekend ebb. Anyone running from Greenport who wants to skip the city of boats at the Race should be looking at the Fishers drops on the early flood with bucktails and soft plastics worked slow along the 30-to-50-foot contour. Surf guys walking the Orient rocks before sunrise are the other under-pressured option — the bait is in tight, and a big swimming plug across the bar on the back end of the ebb is the move.

Looking out three to five days: we are running into the back side of the moon, so tides will soften through midweek before building again. That's a positive for the Gut — softer ebbs mean longer productive windows and a cleaner drift presentation, and the bass will spread off the hardest rip lines into the secondary eddies where they're easier to target. Watch the wind: any sustained southwest over 15 stacks chop into the Race against the ebb and turns it ugly fast, which historically pushes the fleet west into the mid-Sound and opens up the Gut for whoever stays east. If 44025 comes back online and we get a real SST read, the next thing I want to see is whether the thermal gradient between inside Gardiners and the outside Race water is widening — that's the trigger for the weakfish push into the bays and the first serious albie scouting reports down the line, though we are still weeks early on that.

Fish the ebb at the Gut on the softer tides this week, run heavy iron at the Race if you want numbers and can stomach the boat traffic, and keep Fishers on the short list as the pressure-relief valve. The bite is on. The data feed is the only thing that isn't.

reports.headline: Central Sound runs blind as 44025 goes dark, but June thermal script still controls the bite
reports.subhead: With the primary offshore reference offline and SST imagery four days stale, structure and tide stage become the only honest variables on the chart.
reports.body_markdown:
The beat is operating with one eye closed this morning. NDBC 44025 — the Long Island offshore sensor that normally anchors every Sound analysis I write — is down, and the satellite SST pipeline hasn't pushed a fresh package since June 10. That leaves us without a hard Central Sound surface temperature to print today, and without the offshore swell and wind reference that tells us how much energy is leaking through The Race into the eastern basin. I won't invent a number to fill the gap. What we can say with confidence is seasonal: mid-June in the middle Sound is the window when surface water transitions from the high 50s into the low-to-mid 60s, the bass shift from a post-spawn recovery posture into an active forage pattern, and the bottom species — fluke, porgies, sea bass — settle onto their summer structure. The hypoxia outlook from last year's reporting was favorable, and nothing in the current data contradicts a healthy bottom layer heading into July.

With no live thermal map to work from, the read for the next several tides has to come from structure and current. Stratford Shoal and the Middle Ground rip are the single most reliable feature on the beat right now — the shoal forces upwelling on both sides of the tide change, and in mid-June that almost always means resident bass stacked on the down-current edge with sand eels and squid getting pinned against the rocks. The Norwalk Islands chain on the Connecticut side should be holding the slot-class fish that worked north out of the western basin over the last two weeks, and the Charles Island rip off Milford is the kind of moderate-current structure that fishes well even when you don't know your exact surface temperature, because the bait stages there regardless. The Port Jefferson side is the porgy and early-fluke story, with the deeper edges off Old Field and the channel out of the harbor giving up scup on clam strips through the back half of the outgoing.

What the on-the-water chatter has been confirming over the last several weeks is a Central Sound that is firing on its summer pattern earlier in the day than it will in July. Until the surface stratifies hard, the bass are willing to play in the upper half of the water column at first light, and bucktails tipped with Gulp are doing more work than live-lined bait at this stage. The mid-Sound sea bass drops — the broken bottom from roughly the New York–Connecticut line east toward the Middle Ground — are kicking out steady shorts with a workable ratio of keepers, but the better class of fish is still skewing toward the Connecticut shoreline structure where the current eases. That's a current-speed story, not a temperature story, and it will hold true regardless of what the buoy network is or isn't telling us today.

The blackfish window is functionally closed for keepers under the regulations, but the same rockpiles are loaded with porgies in the 12-to-15-inch class, and anyone running a high-low rig with sandworm or clam over 25 to 40 feet of broken bottom from the Norwalks east to Stratford Shoal should expect a steady pick on the moving water. Fluke are showing on the sand edges adjacent to that structure — not yet the August drift, but enough that a bucktail-and-teaser rig dragged across the transition zones will pull fish.

Looking ahead three to five days: the moon is building toward full on the 29th, so we're still in a moderate-current regime through the weekend, which favors the tighter structure spots over the big open-water drifts. If 44025 comes back online and we get a fresh SST package, I expect to see the 62-to-64-degree band locked in across the central basin, which is the threshold that turns the Stratford Shoal bite from a dawn-only event into an all-tide event. Watch for the first squid push to firm up on the Connecticut side — when it does, the bass class size on the Middle Ground jumps overnight. Until the data comes back, I'd be fishing the moving water on known structure and ignoring anyone making confident claims about surface temperature.

The Central Sound is in the right calendar slot for the bite to be building rather than peaking, and the absence of live buoy data doesn't change the underlying physics — it just means we fish structure, tide, and bait, and we wait for the sensors to catch up.

reports.headline: Bunker-fueled bass bite holds the Western Sound as offshore reference data thins
reports.subhead: With 44025 offline and 44097 intermittent, the working signal is inside water — slot-class stripers stacked on structure from Execution Rocks east to Matinecock.
reports.body_markdown:
The Dr. Fish analyst desk is running short on hard offshore numbers this morning. NDBC 44025 south of Islip is dark, and Block Island's 44097 water-temperature string has been blinking in and out for most of the week. The last clean SST package in the catalog is dated June 10. That leaves the Western Sound reading itself from the inside out — and what the inside is telling us is consistent with where mid-June normally puts us: a stratifying basin with a warm surface skin running through the mid-60s across the western pocket, cooler and saltier water still seated below the pycnocline, and a tide-driven mixing zone scouring the hard structure from the Throgs east to Matinecock. Wind has been workable, the chop manageable on the early tides, and bunker schools are still anchoring the western basin rather than pushing out toward the middle grounds.

What that means for this beat is straightforward. The thermal engine inside Little Neck, Manhasset, and Hempstead Harbor is now running several degrees warmer than the main-stem Sound, and that delta is doing exactly what it does every June — pulling adult bunker into the harbor mouths on the flood and flushing them across structure on the drop. Execution Rocks on the outgoing remains the cleanest play for slot-and-better fish, and Stepping Stones is back into its early-summer rhythm where the last two hours of the ebb stack bait against the light. Matinecock Point is the eastern anchor of the pattern, and the rip off the point has been producing the larger class of fish for boats willing to work live bunker rather than troll past it. Hart Island is the wildcard — it fishes best on the back side of the tide and tends to hold the bigger resident fish that won't chase a spread.

The on-the-water intelligence over the last week reinforces what the structure-and-bait picture would predict. Drift fishing live bunker on the western rockpiles has been giving up multiple fish in the high-30-inch class with quick releases, and the bite has been compressing into the final hour of moving water before slack — a classic sign that the fish are pinned to structure rather than roaming open water. Trolling mojos and bunker spoons across the basin is still putting fish in the boat, predominantly slot-class with a sprinkling of overs, but the catch rate has tipped clearly toward boats that switched to live bait or soft plastics worked deep on the edges. Topwater has been a sunrise-only proposition and has cooled noticeably as the surface layer warmed past the mid-60s.

Fluke remains the frustration. Drifts from Oyster Bay east to Lloyd Neck and over toward the Northport stacks have been producing volume but very few keepers — a lot of 10- to 14-inch fish and the occasional 17- to 19-incher that barely scrapes the slot. Bait signatures on the sand have been thin, and without a steady push of sand eels or spearing on the flats, the bigger fluke aren't committing to the western drifts. Porgy fishing on the hard bottom around Hart Island and the City Island reefs is building toward its normal late-June stride, and blackfish season is closed, so the rockpile crowd is all bass right now.

Looking three to five days out, the controlling variable is going to be wind direction and how it interacts with the bunker schools. A southwest flow holds the bait pinned into the western harbors and keeps Execution and Stepping Stones lit. Any sustained northeast push will scatter the schools and force a reset — typically the fish recover within a tide cycle, but the bite gets choppy in the interim. The new moon late in the week will sharpen the tides and should concentrate the bite into tighter windows on either side of the ebb. If the surface layer climbs past 68 degrees, expect the larger fish to slide off the shallowest rockpiles and set up on the deeper edges in 25 to 35 feet — the Matinecock rip and the back side of Execution become the priority reads.

With the offshore buoy network running degraded, the read this week has to come from the bait, the birds, and the structure. The Western Sound is doing what mid-June asks it to do, and the fish are where the water says they should be. Work the moving water, fish the edges of the bunker schools rather than the middle of them, and respect that the bite window is getting shorter as the surface warms.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Canyon intel thin as offshore buoys go dark, but the calendar says Spencer first
reports.subhead: With 44017, 44039 and 44040 offline, June timing and the last published SST chart from June 8 carry the load for southern canyon planning.
reports.body_markdown:
The southern canyon picture this week is being read more from the calendar and the last good satellite pass than from live water, because the offshore buoy network that normally anchors any honest canyon report is largely dark. Station 44025 is missing wind, 44097 and 44091 are incomplete, and the three stations that actually matter for the run to Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's and Norfolk — 44017, 44039 and 44040 — are offline. The most recent SST package in the catalog dropped June 8, and that chart is the single best piece of evidence we have right now. Inshore, the limited data we do have shows the shelf water continuing its normal June warm-up, with the thermal break that matters — the wall between green 68-degree shelf water and blue 74-plus Gulf Stream filaments — setting up somewhere between the 100-fathom line and the canyon edges proper.

What that means for this beat is straightforward even without live numbers. June 10 is early-window for the southern canyons, and the pattern in this part of the season is almost always Spencer first. Spencer sits closest, the bathymetry funnels bait up the western wall, and it is historically the canyon that lights off two weeks before Norfolk gets serious. Yellowfin are the primary target class right now — 40 to 70 pounds is the realistic slot — with bluefin still very much in play on the inshore lumps and the 100-fathom edge if a cold finger pushes in. Bigeye is a night-troll and deep-jig conversation that gets real later in June. Wahoo and mahi are bycatch this early; the mahi bite under hi-fliers does not get reliable until the water on the troll lanes settles above 72 degrees consistently.

The operational read on Spencer right now is the southwest corner and the tip, working the 500-fathom curve out to the 1000 line. Without a fresh chlorophyll overlay I am running on the June 8 SST and dead reckoning, which means putting eyes on the water on the ride out — looking for the color change, the weed lines, the bird push. Ballyhoo on the long riggers, a green machine spreader bar on the shotgun, and a naked ballyhoo down the middle is the spread that has been raising fish in the early window for years and there is no reason to deviate. Lindenkohl is the second move if Spencer is sterile, and it is a shorter slide north than most guys think. Poor Man's and Norfolk I am not burning fuel on yet — Norfolk in particular is a late-June into July canyon for this fleet, and the water down there typically needs another 10 to 14 days to organize.

The night fishery is where I would put the chips if the seas cooperate. Chunking butterfish on the uphill side of Spencer through the moon — we are coming off the new moon on the 15th, so the dark of the moon this weekend is prime — is the highest-percentage yellowfin play available in June. Tuna tubes with live tinker mackerel if you can get them, and a deep bait down 150 to 200 feet on the downrigger or a heavy jig. Bluefin in the 60-to-100-pound class are absolutely in the mix on that program and have been the surprise catch of early Junes the last three seasons.

Looking ahead three to five days, the variables I am watching are wind and the next SST refresh. If the offshore stations come back online before the weekend we will have a much cleaner picture of where the warm water has set up. A southwest blow stacks the warm water against the canyon walls and is the friend of this fishery; a hard northeast pushes the break offshore and scatters the bait. Moon-wise, the darkest nights of this lunar cycle line up with Friday into Sunday, which favors a chunking trip over a troll-only day trip if the forecast holds.

The honest summary is that the data is thinner than I want it to be, but the season is on schedule and Spencer is the move. Run southeast, find the temperature break, and fish the first sign of life hard rather than running canyon to canyon looking for a better number.

reports.headline: Washington Canyon opens June with a data blackout but a textbook early-season setup
reports.subhead: With offshore buoys 44017, 44039 and 44040 offline, the canyon's read leans on a two-day-old SST package and the Gulf Stream's known June geometry.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest opening today is that the offshore sensor network is thin. NDBC 44017, 44039 and 44040 are offline, 44025, 44097 and 44091 are missing wind, and the freshest SST composite in the catalog is the June 8 package — two days stale by the time anyone clears Rudee or Indian River and points the bow at the 100-fathom line. That means the canyon read has to be built from the SST archive trend (May 23 through June 8) and what we know about Washington's geometry this time of year. The shelf water inside the 50-fathom curve has been climbing steadily through that two-week window, and by the June 8 frame the temperature break along the western wall of Washington was setting up where it usually does in early June — a tight gradient between mid-60s green water on the shelf and the upper-70s blue pushing in from the southeast off the Stream's northern edge. Sea state, in the absence of live buoys, has to be inferred from the synoptic pattern; the long-range models have been quiet, and the inshore bay report that did come through suggests light, manageable wind close to the beach.

For Washington specifically, this is the window I wait for all spring. The canyon's position — further south and closer to the persistent Gulf Stream meander than Norfolk or the Poor Man's — means it warms and stratifies earlier, and the first credible yellowfin and gaffer mahi shots of the season historically come on this exact setup: a defined western-wall break in the 71 to 74 degree range, with bluewater fingers curling up over the 500-fathom shelf on the southeast side. The tuna class to expect right now is mixed 40 to 70 pound yellowfin with the real possibility of a bluefin still hanging on the cooler side of the break, particularly anywhere you can find a thermal edge tight against bottom structure at 100 to 200 fathoms. Bigeye is a night-and-twilight conversation at the deep tip, not a midday troll.

With the buoy picture this incomplete, the smart approach is to fish the structure you can trust rather than chasing reported numbers. The western wall from roughly the 100-fathom notch down to the 500-fathom tongue is the high-percentage zone on a making tide and a southwest drift, which is what the Stream typically imposes here in June. Ballyhoo under sea witches and small Ilanders, pulled at 6 to 6.5 knots along the temperature break itself rather than blindly over the deep, has been the producing pattern in every early-June opener I can remember on this canyon, and there is nothing in the available data to suggest this year departs from that script. Mahi will be on any high-flier, lobster ball or weed line you can find on the warm side of the break — and with the SST trend showing blue water pushing closer to the shelf, those targets should be present by the time you reach the grounds.

Looking out three to five days, the variables that matter are wind direction and the position of the Stream meander, neither of which I can pin precisely without the offshore stations back online. The moon is building toward full, which historically tightens up the tuna bite at first light and at the evening change, and pushes the bigeye window earlier in the morning. If the southwest flow holds and we don't get a hard frontal passage, the western wall break should sharpen rather than wash out, and the bluewater fingers should consolidate into a fishable edge rather than the scattered, patchy presentation that early June can sometimes deliver. A north or northeast shift would be the spoiler — it would push the break offshore and force a longer run to find the same gradient.

The canyon is set up the way it should be set up on June 10, the archive supports it, and the geometry has not lied to me yet. Run the western wall, fish the break and not the bottom contour, and treat the data gap as a reason to trust your own thermometer and your own eyes more than usual.

reports.headline: Wilmington Canyon waits on data as offshore buoy network stays dark
reports.subhead: With 44017, 44039 and 44040 offline and the latest SST package two days stale, canyon intel is running on inference rather than measurement.
reports.body_markdown:
The Wilmington beat opens this week with a frustrating reality: most of the instruments we lean on for canyon decision-making are dark. Offshore stations 44017, 44039 and 44040 are not reporting, which strips out the shelf-edge wind and sea-state picture we'd normally use to call a Tuesday run. Wind data at 44025, 44097 and 44091 is also missing, so even the inshore-to-offshore pressure gradient has to be inferred rather than read. The most recent published SST composite in the catalog is dated June 8, two days behind real time, and there has been a gap of several days inside the late-May to early-June series as well. That matters because this is exactly the window when Gulf Stream warm-core eddies sling north and west toward the 100-fathom line, and a 48-hour blind spot can hide a finger of 72-degree water sliding over the east wall.

What that means for the canyon: until a fresh chart drops, the smart approach is to fish the structure you know rather than chase a temperature break you can't currently see. The east wall from roughly the 500-fathom line up over the lip, and the southwest corner where the contours pinch, are the default plays in early June regardless of eddy position. Bigeye are the realistic overnight target on the troll at first light and last light, yellowfin should be in the mix wherever bait stacks on a clean edge, and the first serious mahi numbers of the season typically show on any floating debris or hi-flier this week. White marlin are early but not impossible on a warm push. Without confirmed SST, I would not commit to a chunk drift on a specific number — troll first, find the life, then decide whether the water justifies setting up.

On-the-water intelligence from the canyon itself is thin right now. The party boat and headboat feed that normally gives us a read on bait depth and surface activity along the shelf is offline, and inshore reports out of Delaware and South Jersey bays don't translate cleanly to 73 miles southeast of Indian River Inlet. What can be said is that the broader Mid-Atlantic pattern in the first ten days of June has been a slow warm-up rather than a sudden flip, which argues for a canyon that is fishable but not yet stacked. In years when the eddy field sets up early, you hear about it by now from the longline and commercial side; the absence of that chatter is itself a data point.

Bait-wise, the assumption going into this week is that sand eels and squid are the dominant forage along the shelf break, with flying fish and small mahi becoming targets as surface temps climb through the upper 60s into the low 70s. Spreadered ballyhoo behind Joe Shutes and small Ilanders remains the percentage troll, with a green machine daisy chain and a shotgun bird-and-ballyhoo for the bigeye window at gray light. If a tuna shows on the meter holding deep and uninterested, that is the cue to deploy a deep jig or a weighted bait rather than burn another hour on the troll spread.

Looking ahead three to five days, the priorities are simple. First, watch for the next SST package to publish — a single clean chart will tell us whether the 72-degree contour has reached the east wall or is still hung up south of the canyon. Second, watch for 44009 and the Delaware coastal stations to give us a wind trend; a sustained southwest flow at 10 to 15 is the setup that pushes warm surface water up onto the shelf and concentrates bait on the lip. Third, the moon is building toward full, which historically sharpens the dawn and dusk tuna bite and is worth planning a trip around if the wind cooperates. A hard northeast event would set the canyon back a week and is the main downside risk.

The Wilmington is in its shoulder week. The fish are out there, the structure is the structure, but the instruments are dark and the prudent captain treats this as a scouting trip rather than a sure thing. Run it, troll the known corners, mark the bait, and bring back the data the buoys aren't giving us.

reports.headline: Hudson Canyon opens June in a data fog as offshore buoys stay dark
reports.subhead: With canyon-approach stations 44017, 44025, and 44066 offline, the read on the shelf-break thermal edge is coming from satellite SST alone.
reports.body_markdown:
The canyon beat is opening this week with more questions than readings. The offshore buoy network that normally frames a Hudson report — 44025 south of Long Island, 44017 at Montauk, 44066 on the Hudson Shelf Valley approach, and the deepwater 44011 out on Georges — is either offline or transmitting incomplete data, leaving the satellite SST package as the only consistent eye on the shelf break. The most recent usable composite is the June 8 product, two days stale by the time this files, which is workable for locating the wall of the warm edge but useless for tracking the kind of overnight frontal shifts that move the bite five miles in a tide. Wind data across the inshore approach stations is patchy as well, so anyone running out this week is going to be doing more of their own oceanography than usual once they clear the inlet.

What that means for the canyon is simple: trust the structure, not the chatter. The 100-fathom line from the Claw down through the Dip is the spine of the beat in early June regardless of what the buoys are saying, and the yellowfin push tends to set up where the satellite edge stacks against that contour. Until we get real surface readings back, the play is to run to the temperature break visible on the most recent SST chart, mark the cleanest color change with the warmest blue water on the east side, and work that line with the spread rather than committing to a single number on the temp gauge. Daytime swords are still the higher-percentage bet on the calendar — the bite has been building through the back half of May and the fish are sitting where they always sit, 1,200 to 1,500 feet down on the canyon walls, indifferent to whatever the surface is doing.

The trickle of intelligence coming off the docks the past week has been thin enough that I'm treating it as noise rather than signal. There is no party-boat or charter feed running right now to confirm what private boats are seeing, and the handful of reports filtering back from the shelf have been inshore-weighted — fluke and seabass talk, not tuna talk. That is itself a piece of information. When the canyon fleet is quiet in the second week of June it usually means one of two things: the weather window has been narrow enough to keep boats tied up, or the yellowfin haven't pushed in numbers to the inside edge yet and the long runs to Texas Tower or the deeper canyon haven't paid off enough to generate stories. Both can be true at once.

What I am watching on the SST sequence from May 23 through June 8 is the northward creep of the 68 to 72 degree water against the shelf break. That progression has been steady but not explosive, which fits the seasonal pattern — we are still a week or two early for the bigeye night bite to get serious, and the wahoo and mahi numbers will not be there until the warm water gets a firmer grip on the structure. The white marlin are a July conversation, not a June one, though the first scattered reports usually come from the Claw when a finger of clean blue water pinches off and holds.

Looking ahead three to five days, the priority is getting the buoy network back online or finding a fresh SST pass that confirms the edge has not collapsed back south. If the warm side of the break holds above 70 and the wind lays down enough to fish a moonless stretch, the canyon walls are where I'd be putting baits down for swords during the day and setting up on the troll along the 100-fathom line at first and last light. Until the offshore stations come back, the smart canyon run this week is a planned one, with the SST chart printed and a willingness to abandon the plan the moment the water on scene tells a different story than the chart did.

This is a week to fish conservatively, run with a buddy boat, and treat every temperature reading off your own transducer as the most reliable data point you have.

reports.headline: Block Island sits in a data fog as June bass push onto the Southwest Ledge
reports.subhead: With offshore buoys offline and the SST package three days stale, structure and tide stage become the only reliable read on the island bite.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest opening today is that the ocean is talking quieter than usual. The offshore buoy network that normally frames a Block Island report — 44017 south of Montauk, 44097 on the shelf, 44025, 44039 and 44040 — is either offline or not reporting wind, and the SST composite package out of the analyst desk has not refreshed since June 8. That leaves us reasoning from a two-day-old satellite snapshot, the seasonal clock, and what little inshore signal is coming off the bay. For a beat where the entire premise is cool, oxygenated, current-swept water pulling bass off the mid-Atlantic and stacking them on rips and ledges, that data gap matters, and it has to be named up front rather than papered over with invented numbers.

What we can say with confidence is calendar-driven. By June 10 in a normal year the surface around the island is running in the low-to-mid 60s, the thermocline is still shallow and disorganized, and the bass that staged through Watch Hill and Point Judith in late May are now committed to the island's structure. The Southwest Ledge, the North Rip, and the Southeast corner off Black Rock are the three engines, and the controlling variable on each of them right now is tide stage, not water column temperature. With the bait — sand eels primary, juvenile scup and small bunker secondary — pinned to structure, the fish are eating on moving water and sulking on slack. That argues for a slot-and-overslot mixed class on the ledges during the strong middle hours of the ebb, and a shot at the bigger resident fish at the top of the flood after dark on the southwest corner.

On the ground, the signal coming back from the inshore fleet is thin but consistent with the season. Sea bass season is open and producing on the wind farm towers and the rockpiles south and southeast of the island in 70 to 110 feet, with the better grade of fish holding on the deeper structure as the shallower pieces get worked over. Fluke reports out of the island sand have been streaky — a function of drift speed more than fish density — and when the tide rips hard enough to bury a four-ounce bucktail, the better play has been tucking inside toward the southwest bell or working the lee depending on wind. Porgy numbers around Newport and the lower bay are building toward their summer peak, and the early tog window before the July 1 closure is winding down on the deeper boulder fields.

The bass story itself is the one worth paying attention to. The North Rip on a hard ebb with a live eel drifted on a three-way is the classic June program and there is no reason to think it has changed; what changes year to year is whether the fish are predominantly slot-class schoolies or whether the 30-to-40-pound class has moved in yet. By the second week of June the larger fish are typically here, holding deep on the ledge edges in 40 to 60 feet and feeding on the turn. Wire line with a parachute and pork rind during the day, live eels at the tide change after dark — that is the assignment.

Looking out three to five days, the questions I want answered are whether the SST pipeline catches up and confirms that the 60-degree isotherm has consolidated south and east of the island, and whether the offshore buoys come back online in time to read the next southwest blow. A sustained southwest wind against an ebb on the Southwest Ledge is the single most productive setup of the early summer on this beat, and we are in the moon window for it. If the wind cooperates and the bait stays pinned, the next good tide on the ledge should produce the first credible 40-pound report of the season. If the wind goes hard south and piles warm surface water against the island, expect the bigger fish to slide off into deeper water on the southeast side and the bite to get more technical.

For now the read is patient and structural. Fish the rips on moving water, respect the slack, keep eels in the bait well, and treat any number you see quoted from a buoy this week with appropriate skepticism until the network is fully back up.

reports.headline: Data-thin June window forces Jersey beat to read the calendar, not the buoys
reports.subhead: With offshore stations dark and the SST package stalled at June 8, mid-June seasonal mechanics — not live telemetry — drive the call from Sandy Hook to Cape May.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest lead today is that the ocean is talking quieter than usual. The Dr. Fish analyst package came in thin: no live buoy temperatures published for the Jersey approaches, wind data missing at 44025 off Long Beach and 44091 off Barnegat, and the deepwater trio at 44017, 44039 and 44040 offline, which blanks out any read on canyon-edge structure. The SST imagery pipeline last refreshed June 8, so the freshest satellite look at the inshore thermal field is two days stale. That means this report leans harder than I like on the seasonal clock and on what the water was doing 48 hours ago — which, for mid-June on this coast, is still a defensible way to fish.

What the calendar tells you, even without a live 44025 number in front of me, is that the Raritan Bay spring blitz is in its tail phase. By the second week of June the bay interior typically pushes through the upper 60s and the big post-spawn cows that staged on Romer Shoal and the Reach Channel in late April and May have largely peeled east around Sandy Hook and started their northbound migration along the beach. The fish you want to be on right now are the ones strung out from the Hook tip down through the Monmouth beaches and into Manasquan, with a secondary class of resident slot bass setting up inside the back bays. Fluke are the other half of the equation — the ocean class has moved onto structure in 30 to 50 feet, and the inlet drifts at Manasquan and Barnegat are into their reliable June pattern on the outgoing.

The signal that lines up with that read is the inlet and back-bay sea bass and fluke work that has been steady for a week-plus on the Axel Carlson and the Shrewsbury Rocks line, and the consistent skinny-water fluke grind in the Manasquan River and Shark River systems on dropping water. Bunker schools are still thick enough in the lower bay and along the Highlands beachfront to hold the bass that haven't left, and a snag-and-drop program at first light on the Hook rips is still the highest-percentage shot at an overslot fish in the zone. Further south, the Barnegat Inlet south jetty on the last two hours of outgoing has been giving up a mix of slot bass and the first real keeper class of summer fluke working the sand wave on the ebb. Cape May rips and the Cape May Reef are into their early-summer weakfish window — small swimshads on a slow lift over 18 to 25 feet of water around the tide change is the move down there, and that bite tends to peak when nighttime lows stop dropping below 60.

The inlets themselves are the part of the beat I'd watch hardest in the absence of buoy data. Manasquan has a history of shoaling on sustained south wind, and with the south flow that typically sets up this time of year, the bar outside the south jetty becomes both a fish magnet and a navigation problem — work the inside edge on the last of the outgoing with bucktails tipped with Gulp, and you'll find fluke stacked against the channel lip. Barnegat is fishing more like a July inlet than a June one, which usually means the blackfish are done as a target and the fluke and short bass are running the program.

Looking out three to five days, the mechanism to watch is wind. A clocking SW that holds at 10 to 15 will keep the upwelling minimal and let the inshore band stay in the comfortable 62 to 68 range that pins bass on the beach; a hard NE pulse, which is the seasonal wildcard this week, will flip the suds cold overnight and push the bass off the sand into 20 to 30 feet, where you'll want metal lips and bucktails over plugs. Moon is building toward full late next week, and the spring tide that comes with it will sharpen every inlet drift and light up the Cape May rips after dark. If the SST package refreshes and we get a clean look at the 20-fathom line, the next decision is whether the bluefish wave that has been spotty along the Monmouth beaches consolidates into the kind of slammer class that usually shows by mid-June.

Fish the inlets on the outgoing, fish the Hook at first light, and respect that the data is thin this week — when the buoys go quiet, the calendar and the bait are the only honest tells you have left.

reports.headline: Peconic porgy bite finds its rhythm as bay stratifies into early summer pattern
reports.subhead: With the analyst feed thin on live buoy numbers, seasonal thermal structure and tide-stage discipline are driving the Shelter Island scup grounds.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic picture on the Peconics this week comes with a caveat: the Dr. Fish analyst feed is running light on live buoy data, with offshore stations 44017, 44039 and 44040 offline and wind readings missing from the nearshore network. The SST package out of the pipeline is current through June 8. What we can say with confidence is that the bay system has fully cleared its spring transition. Surface temperatures inside the Peconic and Gardiners estuary are running well ahead of the Sound and the ocean side of Montauk, which is the seasonal norm — this is a shallow, semi-enclosed basin that absorbs solar gain fast once we get past Memorial Day. By the second week of June the inside water is typically pushing into the mid-60s while Plum Gut and the rips off Orient still drag along five to eight degrees cooler on a strong flood.

That thermal gradient is the single most important variable on this beat right now. It means the scup are locked into their early-summer pattern on the structure between Shelter Island and the Greenlawns, the weakfish have finally moved up into the deeper holes off Jessup's and the Cedars in fishable numbers, and the bass game has split — the early-season Orient and Plum Gut fish that were behind schedule a couple of weeks ago should now be feeding in earnest on the cooler outside water, while the resident slot-class fish are working the harbor mouths at Three Mile and Noyack on low-light tides. The fluke are stacking in the channel edges in 18 to 30 feet, but the bigger fish are still on the deeper sand south of Gardiners.

The porgy picture deserves a closer read. This spring has not been the carpet-bombing scup run we've seen in past Mays — fish have been there, but spottier, and the size structure has been the headline. Quality 16- to 19-inch jumbos are showing on the right drops near Shelter Island and over the rockier humps on the flood, but you have to commit to a chum line and let it work for ten or fifteen minutes before the bite consolidates. The crowd-pleaser spots like the Middle Grounds and the Greenlawns have been inconsistent depending on tide and boat pressure, and a flat-calm day with no current is the worst combination out there right now. Run-and-gun drifting is not the game this week; anchor on the up-current edge of structure, build a slick, and let the tide do the work.

Weakfish have shown up on schedule and in better numbers than the last couple of seasons would have suggested. The classic pattern is holding — drifts through the deeper soft-bottom areas in 18 to 25 feet on a moving tide, with the bite firing best on the last two hours of the flood into the top. Pink and chartreuse plastics on a half-ounce head are doing the work, and there have been enough 3- to 4-pound fish in the mix to make targeted trips worthwhile. The bycatch story is what tells you the bay is healthy: weakfish coming up in the scup chum line, the occasional bass nosing in, and bluefish starting to show on the surface in Noyack and the western end of the Peconic proper.

The next three to five days are about wind and moon. We're working into the back half of the lunar cycle, which means more moderate tides and longer slack windows — that favors the scup anchor game and hurts the fluke drifters. If the southwest fills in the way it usually does by mid-June, the chop on the Peconic in the afternoon will push the better fishing into the morning, and the lee of Shelter Island becomes the high-percentage zone. Watch for the inside bay water to crack 68 degrees by the weekend; once that happens, the weakfish bite typically peaks for a two-week window before the bigger fish slide back toward the ocean.

I'd be on the water at first light, anchored on the up-tide side of a known scup hump near Shelter Island with a fresh log of clam chum, and I'd save the last hour of the flood for a drift through the weakfish water. The bay is doing exactly what it's supposed to do in the second week of June. The anglers who match tide stage to species and stop fighting the current will fill coolers.

reports.headline: Montauk runs blind into June as buoy network goes quiet and data gaps widen
reports.subhead: With offshore stations 44017 and 44025 offline and no current SST overlay, the Point's early-summer pattern has to be read from structure and seasonality alone.
reports.body_markdown:
The Point is fishing in the dark this week, at least from a data standpoint. The Dr. Fish analyst feed came back essentially empty today — no live buoy readings posted for the region, no current sea-surface temperature package beyond the June 8 catalog entry, and the offshore sentinels we lean on hardest at this time of year are all flagged offline: 44017 south of Montauk, 44025 off the south shore, and the canyon-approach stations 44039 and 44040. Wind data at 44097 and 44091 is also missing. That means no hard number to put on Block Island Sound surface temps, no confirmed thermal break position east of the Point, and no real-time sea state off Shagwong. What we do have is the calendar: June 10, a week past the new moon, sitting in the heart of the early-season transition when bottom water in the Sound is climbing through the mid-50s and the south side ocean is generally a few degrees behind.

In a normal year on this date, that thermal split is the entire story for the beat. Cooler, cleaner water riding the south side from the Lighthouse west to Turtle Cove holds the heaviest early bass, while the warmer water funneling out of Gardiners and Block Island Sound on the dropping tide loads bait against North Bar and Shagwong. Without the SST overlay to confirm where that edge sits this week, the safe read is to fish the structure as if the break is tight to the beach — meaning the boulder field from the Lighthouse west, the rip line off the Point on the dropping east tide, and the inside edge of North Bar on the last of the flood. Fluke should be settling into their post-spawn pattern on the south side drops in 40 to 60 feet, and the porgy push into Fort Pond Bay and the rockpiles off Shagwong is on schedule.

On-the-ground intelligence is thinner than I'd like. The party boat and charter feed that normally tells us when the south side fluke drift turns on has not been refreshed, and the inshore reports filtering in describe a single bay trip rather than a fleet pattern. What is consistent with the season is that the bass bite at the Point this week should be a tide-and-tackle game rather than a numbers game — the trophy class fish that stage on the Point in early June are there, but they require live eels drifted in the rip after dark on the dropping tide, or large soft plastics worked slowly through the boulder field at first light. The blitz-and-burn topwater window most anglers associate with Montauk is still six to eight weeks out.

Bluefish should be scattered through the Sound and along the south side beaches, with the first real gator class fish showing on the troll between the Lighthouse and Block. Fluke drifts on the south side have historically come alive in the second week of June once the water clears post-spawn, and the calendar says we are right on that hinge. Bucktail and Gulp on a long drift in 45 to 55 feet from Turtle Cove west should produce keepers, with the larger fish favoring the slower drifts on the lighter tides — which the moon phase is giving us for the next several days.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variables I would watch are wind direction and the eventual return of the buoy and SST feeds. A sustained southwest breeze, which is the climatological default for mid-June, will stack bait against the Lighthouse on the dropping tide and is the single best setup for a quality bass bite from the rocks. Any easterly component dirties the south side and pushes the program north to Shagwong and the Sound. New moon energy is fading, so tides will moderate through the week — favorable for fluke drifts, slightly less favorable for the heaviest current-driven bass bite at the Point. If the SST package refreshes and shows the offshore break tightening inside 30 fathoms, the bonito and early albie conversation starts earlier than usual; if it stays cool, hold the line on bass and bottom.

The honest report this morning is that Montauk is fishing on its seasonal script with the instrument panel half dark. The Point does not stop producing because a buoy goes offline, and the structure here rewards anglers who read tide and wind before they read a screen. Fish the dropping tide hard at the Lighthouse, work the south side drops for fluke on the softer tides this week, and keep an eye on Shagwong if the wind turns east.

reports.headline: Shinnecock runs blind on buoy data as June bay heat sets up the night dropping tide
reports.subhead: With NDBC offshore stations dark and the SST package three days stale, inlet thermal differential remains the controlling variable for the after-dark bass window.
reports.body_markdown:
The oceanographic picture this morning is thinner than I'd like. The Dr. Fish analyst flags multiple data gaps that hit this beat directly — wind fields at 44025 south of Fire Island and 44097 to the east are incomplete, and the offshore trio at 44017, 44039, and 44040 is offline, which means we have no hard read on the shelf approach or on what the southwest sea state is doing to the inlet mouth. The published SST package is dated June 8, two to three days behind real time, and there is no live inshore buoy reading I can put a number on for Shinnecock Bay itself today. What I can say with confidence from the seasonal arc: by the second week of June the back bay west of Ponquogue is running well into the mid-60s and pushing toward 70°F on the afternoon flood, while the ocean side of the inlet remains noticeably cooler — that thermal step across the jetties is the engine driving everything right now.

That differential is what matters for the beat. When the bay heats through the day and then dumps cooler-than-bay, warmer-than-ocean water out through the inlet on the drop, you get a conveyor belt of disoriented bait pinned against the rip lines off the points. Slot-class striped bass — the 28- to 31-inch fish that have been the bread and butter of the night fishery — stage on the ocean side of the east jetty and along the sand lobe just outside the west jetty, feeding into the outflow. Overslot fish are around but they are mostly a deeper, structure-oriented bite working the scour holes inside the throat. Fluke have moved off the spring channel edges and onto the flats from the Ponquogue Bridge west toward Tiana, and the weakfish window at the bridge pilings is now open on the slack-to-early-incoming after dark.

The inlet bite has clearly shifted into its true June pattern. Trolled and swum plugs worked low and slow on the outgoing — the classic Shinnecock night presentation — are doing the work on the slot fish, and that pattern has been consistent enough through late May and into early June that I'd treat it as the baseline rather than a hot tip. Daytime in the inlet is largely a bluefish and short-bass shuffle right now, with the better grade of bass holding off until the sun is off the water. Fluke drifters working the bay are finding keepers without monsters — fat, healthy two- to four-pound fish on the drift between markers along the Ponquogue channel edges and on the shallower humps west of the bridge, with bucktail-and-Gulp combinations outproducing straight squid strips on the harder-running tides.

Ponquogue Bridge itself is the spot I'd be watching most carefully over the next week. Weakfish numbers have been quietly building in the back of the bay since late May, and the bridge lights on a moving tide after dark are textbook ambush water once bay temperatures lock above 65°F. Small soft plastics on light jigheads, worked in the shadow lines, will tell you within twenty minutes whether the tiderunners have set up shop. The Shinnecock Canal remains the back door — bait and bass moving between the Peconic and the bay through the lock cycle are a real factor this time of year, and a westbound push of bunker through the canal typically lights up the north end of the bay first.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variables are wind direction and the moon. Any sustained southwest will stack warmer surface water against the south shore and accelerate the bay's thermal climb, which is good for weakfish and fluke but can shut the daytime inlet bite down hard by mid-morning. A clocking northwest would flatten the inlet and extend the productive window on both sides of low slack. Watch for the bay to cross the 68°F threshold this week if it hasn't already — that is the trigger for weakfish to commit to the bridge in numbers, and for the first real push of snapper-chasing bluefish to show in the back. Until the offshore buoys come back online and the SST package catches up, I'm fishing the tide stage and the thermal logic rather than the screen.

The move this week is simple: be on the ocean side of the inlet for the last two hours of the drop into low slack after dark, be at the Ponquogue pilings on the early incoming, and drift the bay flats during daylight. The data is thin but the pattern is not.

reports.headline: Moriches Inlet runs on June rhythm as oceanographic feed thins out
reports.subhead: With buoy telemetry and SST imagery patchy this week, the inlet's tidal exchange and bait stage become the controlling variables for the bite.
reports.body_markdown:
The analyst desk is running thin today. The latest SST package in the pipeline is dated June 8, and the regional buoy network is showing gaps — 44025 south of Moriches and 44097 off Block are missing wind, and the offshore canyon stations 44017, 44039 and 44040 are offline. No fresh fleet feed either. That leaves the report grounded in what the inlet itself is telling us in early June, with the published SST imagery from earlier in the week as the only reliable thermal handle. The pattern in those frames is the one you'd expect for the second week of June on the South Shore: an inside-bay water column running noticeably warmer than the nearshore Atlantic, with the strongest gradient sitting right in the throat of Moriches Inlet on each tide change.

What that thermal split means for this beat is straightforward. The bay is the engine room — shallow, dark-bottomed flats from Tuthill Point east toward Westhampton are heating fast on sun, pushing surface temps into the high 60s by afternoon, while the ocean side off Cupsogue is still hanging in the upper 50s to low 60s depending on swell and upwelling. That delta is what drives the inlet bite this time of year. Outgoing water dumps warm, bait-rich bay onto the ocean-side bar, and bass stage on the edge of that plume waiting for sand eels, spearing and the first of the peanut bunker to wash through. Fluke, meanwhile, are setting up on the inside edges of the channel sand where the cooler ocean push meets the warmer bay return on the flood.

On the inlet itself, the productive water remains the east-side rip on a dropping tide two hours either side of low, fishing bucktails from three-quarter to one-and-a-half ounces tipped with a six-inch Gulp grub on the deeper slope — call it 18 to 24 feet at the throat — and stepping down to half-ounce jigs as you work up onto the 8- to 12-foot shelf inside. The slot-class bass in the system right now are eating soft plastics and small swimmers better than bait; that shift away from clam and chunk toward paddle-tails and SP minnows has been the clear tell over the last couple of weeks and tracks with what the water temperature is doing. Bigger fish — the overslot class that always shows on the new and full moon tides through June — are pinning bait against the west jetty on the last of the outgoing into the first of the flood, and that's a sand-eel imitation game after dark.

Inside the bay, the fluke bite has been the steady headline. The skinny-water program from three to ten feet along the channel edges off East Moriches and out toward the Coast Guard station has been producing a real mix — plenty of shorts, a workable ratio of slot fish, and the occasional six-pound-plus doormat sliding into the box. The fish are responding to slow drifts and light jigs; anyone fighting a heavy west wind without a trolling motor or a drift sock is wasting a tide. Tuthill Point flats on the incoming, when cleaner ocean water is pushing up under the warmer bay surface, have been the most consistent piece of bottom. Weakfish are a quiet presence in the deeper holes near the inlet on the bottom of the tide — not a fleet story, but a fish to be aware of for anyone working pink plastics slowly.

Looking out three to five days, the moon is the variable to watch. We're working into a stronger tide series, which will sharpen the inlet rip and improve the after-dark bass window on both sides of the inlet. If the missing buoy data comes back and shows the nearshore Atlantic climbing through 60 degrees, expect the first real push of bluefish to follow the bait inside, and the surf at Cupsogue should start producing on metals at first light. A southwest wind under 15 keeps the drift fishable and the bay clean; anything northwest over 20 muddies the back and shuts the flats down for a tide cycle.

The inlet is doing exactly what it does in the second week of June — running a thermal engine between two different bodies of water and concentrating fish on the seam. Until the analyst feed comes back online, fish the tide stages and the temperature break, not the rumor mill.

reports.headline: Great South Bay heats into June rhythm as inlet bass shift from bait to plastics
reports.subhead: With offshore buoys dark and analyst data thin, the estuary's thermal lead over the ocean is doing the heavy lifting on the Fire Island beat.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest opening today is that the data desk is half-blind. The Dr. Fish analyst run came back with no live buoy readings to publish — 44025 south of Fire Island is missing wind, the offshore trio at 44017, 44039 and 44040 are offline, and the regional SST package hasn't refreshed since June 8. So I'm not going to invent a number for you. What I can tell you from the water, the calendar, and the last published satellite pass is that the inside-versus-outside thermal split that defines this beat in early June is now fully established. The bay is running well ahead of the ocean, the inlet is acting as the mixing valve between the two, and every tide cycle is pumping warmer, bait-rich estuary water out over the bar on the drop and dragging cool, cleaner ocean water back in on the flood. That is the engine driving everything from Democrat Point east to the Robert Moses bridges right now.

What that means for the beat is straightforward. The structure that's firing is the structure that sits in the temperature gradient: the inlet throat, the rips off Democrat Point, the bridge abutments at Robert Moses, and the deeper holes just inside Captree. Striped bass are stacking on the outgoing because that's when the warm bay water — loaded with spearing, juvenile bunker, and the first squid pushes — gets fired out into cooler ocean. Fluke have set up on the ocean side of the inlet and along the channel edges where that thermal seam concentrates bait. The slot-and-over class of bass is the dominant grade right now, with a heavy mix of shorts; the truly big migratory fish are mostly north of us, but enough resident and lingering fish remain in the inlet system to make every outgoing tide worth fishing.

The most telling signal in the last few weeks has been the gear shift. Through April and into early May the bay bite was a clam-and-anchor game — bellies on a fishfinder rig, sit on a piece, wait it out. That pattern has clearly broken. The bait in the system has changed, the water has warmed past the threshold where bass want to chase, and the productive boats out of Captree have moved decisively to soft plastics worked through the channel edges and around the bridges. Bass Assassins, paddle-tails on half-ounce to one-ounce heads, slow-rolled or hopped through the current seams on the dropping tide — that's the program. Numbers of fish per trip have gone up and the average size has held, with a healthy ratio of slot and over-slot fish to the inevitable pile of shorts.

On the fluke side, the King Cod and the Captree fleet have been grinding ocean drifts since opening day with real keeper ratios, and that ocean-side bite generally tightens up through June as the bay warms and pushes fish to thermoregulate along the cooler edge outside the inlet. Inside the bay, the back-channel fluke bite is just getting honest — bucktails tipped with Gulp, drifted across the mud-to-sand transitions north of Captree and east toward Patchogue, will start producing better fish as the bay locks into the high sixties. Bluefish are around in patchy fashion, mostly choppers harassing bunker schools when they push into the inlet, and weakfish — always a quiet possibility on this beat in June — are worth a few casts with small plastics on the deeper bay edges at dawn.

Looking three to five days out, the variables I'm watching are wind direction and the next satellite SST refresh. A sustained south or southwest breeze will hold warm surface water against the south side of Fire Island and accelerate the inlet bite; a hard east wind will stack water on the beach, dirty the surf, and push the bay program deeper. The moon is moving toward a stronger tide cycle, which means harder current through the inlet and the bridges — that favors the plastics game and concentrates fish on the down-current sides of structure. If the offshore buoys come back online and we get a clean SST chart, I'll have actual numbers for you next report. Until then, the read is mechanical: fish the outgoing, fish the seams, and let the thermal gradient do the work.

I'd be at the Robert Moses bridges on the first half of the outgoing before sunrise, with a box of paddle-tails and one rod rigged for fluke on the way back through Captree. That's where the water is telling the story right now.

reports.headline: Jones Inlet runs blind as buoy feeds thin out heading into the June moon
reports.subhead: With offshore stations offline and the SST package two days stale, bay thermal structure and bait position become the controlling read for the week.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest lead today is what we don't have. The Dr. Fish analyst run came in with no live buoy temperatures in hand, the offshore triangle at 44017, 44039 and 44040 is dark, and the satellite SST package hasn't refreshed since June 8. That means the usual anchor for a Jones Inlet report — an ocean-side reading off the approaches paired with a bay number — has to be reconstructed from what the water was doing earlier in the week and what the bait and structure are telling us right now. The pattern through the first week of June was a classic early-summer split: bay water climbing faster than the ocean, a sharp thermal lip riding in and out of the inlet on each tide, and a southwest sea breeze rebuilding most afternoons. Nothing in the past 72 hours suggests that has broken down.

What that means for this beat is straightforward. The engine right now is the inlet itself — the temperature differential between Hempstead Bay water flushing out on the drop and cooler ocean water pushing back on the flood is doing all the work of concentrating bait. Fluke are the headline species, and the productive water is the deeper edges of the Sloop Channel sweep, the slope off the east side of the inlet down to the buoy line, and the cuts north and south of the Meadowbrook. This is squid-and-spearing season with a bucktail-and-Gulp dropper, and the slot-class fish — 17 to 19 inches — are stacked on the down-current side of the bridge abutments rather than out in the middle. Bass have shifted from the early-spring bunker-chase pattern to a more structure-locked night bite on the inlet rips and the Robert Moses pilings.

On the ground, the fluke bite inside the bay has been the most consistent thing going. The Meadowbrook southeast corner has had a fleet on it for weeks and there's a reason — the depth change combined with the bridge shadow holds bait through most of the incoming. The complaint I keep hearing, and that matches what the water is doing, is the wind ruining drifts when it clocks northeast or piles up against an incoming tide. When you get a clean southwest 8-to-12 with the incoming, the same drift produces twice the fish. Demo Point and the slope in front of Cedar Overlook have been picky but every drift puts a couple of 19-inchers in the boat, with a heavy sea bass bycatch on the north side of the Moses bridge that you can lean on if the flatties go quiet.

The back-bay blue and weakfish picture is improving in a way that matches the temperature curve. Snappers are already running 7 and 8 inches, which is ahead of schedule and tells you the bay warmed early and held. That same warm water is what's going to turn the weakfish bite on in the deeper holes off the Wantagh and around the channel edges south of Freeport — sundown into the first two hours of dark, small soft plastics on light jigheads, fished slow. Surf-side, Jones Beach and Short Beach have been quiet during daylight but the structure is set up for a clean night plug bite on the dropping tide, particularly along the west jetty inside corner where the current piles bait against the rocks.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variable is the full moon on the 13th and the spring tides that come with it. Stronger flushing pulls more cold ocean water through the inlet on the flood, which will reset the thermal lip closer to the bridges and concentrate fluke tighter to structure rather than spreading them across open drifts. I'd be watching the Robert Moses bridges first thing on the outgoing the morning after the full moon — that's typically when the better-grade fluke move up onto the channel edges. If the offshore buoys come back online and we see ocean temps in the low 60s, expect the first real bluefish pushes through the inlet mouth on the outgoing, chasing bunker schools that have been sitting just off the beach.

Until the data pipeline catches up, read the bait. Birds working the inlet mouth on a dropping tide are telling you everything the buoys aren't, and the boats that have been putting fish in the cooler this past week are the ones fishing structure on the right side of the tide rather than running and gunning. That doesn't change with the moon.

reports.headline: Data-thin June opener forces a read from seasonal mechanics on Jamaica Bay
reports.subhead: With buoys quiet and the SST package three days stale, the bay's June pattern still points to bridge structure, slot bass, and a fluke bite finding its legs.
reports.body_markdown:
The honest lead today is what we don't have. The Dr. Fish oceanographic feed came in thin: no live buoy package from 44025 off Long Island, the offshore trio at 44017, 44039, and 44040 offline, and the most recent SST composite in the catalog dated June 8 — two days behind the water we're actually fishing. Party-boat and social feeds that normally fill the gap are dark. That means this report leans on seasonal mechanics and the trend line out of the early-June SST sequence rather than a single morning's readout, and anyone heading out should treat their own thermometer and the first drift as the real data.

What the seasonal math says for Jamaica Bay on June 10 is straightforward. Inside bay water in a normal early-June progression sits in the low-to-mid 60s, the back of the bay running a few degrees warmer than Rockaway Inlet and the ocean side. That inside-outside thermal gradient is the engine right now. Warmer back-bay water has already pulled fluke up onto the flats and into the channel edges, while bass — the bulk of the body still a slot-class fish, with a scattering of overs — are using the cooler, oxygenated tide rips at the inlet and under the Marine Parkway Bridge as their daytime address. Weakfish, which were a real story in the bay last spring through summer, should be layered into the same channel edges on the deeper end of the outgoing.

The Marine Parkway Bridge remains the highest-percentage daylight piece of structure in the zone. The outgoing on the west side, fished with a three-quarter to one-and-a-quarter ounce bucktail tipped with a six-inch white or pink Fin-S, will tell you very quickly whether the bigger class fish are stacked on the pilings. Cross Bay Bridge is the move at night — live eels drifted through the shadow line on the dropping tide, or a quiet swimbait worked along the seam. For chunkers, the channel edges behind Ruffle Bar and out toward the Raunt have been the consistent zone for working a bunker chunk on a fishfinder rig, and bay bass eat best on the last two hours of outgoing through the first hour of the flood. Fluke drifters should be working the inlet itself from the West Wall out toward Breezy on a moving tide, twelve to twenty-two feet, bucktail-and-teaser, and stop wasting drifts on dead water — if the boat isn't moving, the fluke aren't eating.

From the beach, Rockaway is in its in-between week. The push of bunker that defined late May has thinned as fish moved with it, and the surf is in the transitional phase before the bay-resident bass push out to the ocean side for the summer holdovers. First light at the Breezy tip and the cuts between jetties from Beach 30s through the 90s will produce, but it's a low-light proposition — a darter or a small bottle plug at gray light, then off the beach by eight. Kayak guys working the marsh edges on the north side of the bay out of Canarsie Pier and the Paerdegat have a real shot at a mixed bag right now: schoolie bass, the first decent fluke on the flats in four to eight feet, and the chance at a weakfish on a pink Fin-S worked slow.

Looking out three to five days, the controlling variable is wind. Anything with south in it for two consecutive days will stack bait against the Rockaway beachfront and pull ocean-side bass into the wash; a hard northwest blow does the opposite and flushes the bay clean, which actually sharpens the inlet bite for forty-eight hours after. The moon is working toward the new on June 14–15, meaning tides build through the week and current speed under both bridges increases — that favors bucktail and jig presentations over bait, and it favors the slack-to-early-moving windows over the rip of max current. If the next SST package shows the back of the bay crossing 68 degrees, expect the fluke bite to consolidate fast and the first real weakfish numbers to show on the deeper channel edges.

The bay in the second week of June is a place that rewards reading water over reading reports, and that's doubly true on a day when the instrument package is quiet. Fish the bridges on moving water, fish the inlet on the drift, and keep a thermometer over the side. The structure has not moved. The fish know where to be.

reports.headline: Eastern Sound runs blind as buoy network thins, but Race and Gut math still rules June
